Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 1:

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The opening of the surah with the report that whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, exalted is He, is a reminder to the believers of their own glorification of Allah, a glorification of gratitude (shukr) for what He granted them of the conquest of the lands of Banu al-Nadir. It is as if He said: "Glorify Allah as whatever is in the heavens and the earth has glorified Him."

It is also an indirect allusion (ta'ridh) to those concerning whom the surah was revealed, that what befell them came about because of their arrogance toward glorifying Allah as He deserves to be glorified, by affirming His Messenger ﷺ, since they turned away from considering the proofs of his prophethood or obstinately denied knowledge of them.

The discussion of the wording of this verse is like the discussion of its counterpart at the beginning of Surah al-Hadid, except that in the beginning of Surah al-Hadid it is ﴿ma fi as-samawati wal-ard﴾ [al-Hashr: 24], whereas here it says ﴿ma fi as-samawati wa ma fil-ard﴾, because the opening of Surah al-Hadid includes evidence for the greatness of Allah, His attributes, and His singularity in creating the heavens and the earth. So the proof of that was the totality of what the heavens and the earth contain of kinds of existing things, and He gathered all of that into a single term, namely the relative pronoun ma, whose relative clause is His saying "in the heavens and the earth." As for the opening of Surah al-Hashr, it was brought to remind of Allah's favour upon the Muslims in an earthly event, namely the humiliation of Banu al-Nadir. So it was fitting there that the people of the earth be singled out by a particular relative pronoun belonging to them, namely the second relative ma, whose relative clause is "in the earth." In this same manner the openings of Surah al-Saff, al-Jumu'ah and al-Taghabun came, as will be explained in their places. The report about ﴿sabbaha lillahi ma fi as-samawati wa ma fil-ard﴾ was expressed with the past tense verb (fi'l al-madi) because what is reported is a glorification of gratitude for a blessing that had passed before the revelation of the surah, namely the blessing of the expulsion of the people of al-Nadir.

﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave.﴾

It is permissible to make the sentence ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved﴾ through to its end an initial resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a topic afresh) for the purpose of extolling God, the Name of Majesty, through this wondrous act of power it contains, and because it implies a reminder that He ought to be thanked for that remarkable expulsion.

It is also permissible to make it the cause (*'illah*) of what the report about the glorification of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth contains, namely a reminder to the believers and an allusion to the People of the Book and the hypocrites, who are two of the groups on the earth, since the story that the opening of the surah contains is among the most important of their circumstances.

It is also permissible to make it an explanation (*mubayyinah*) of the sentence ﴿and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾, because this great subjugation is among the effects of His might and wisdom.

In all cases, it is a reminder of God's blessing upon the Muslims, a hint that they should thank God for it, and a preparation for the purpose of the surah, which is the distribution of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir.

The definition of both parts of the sentence by the pronoun and the relative pronoun (*al-damir wa al-mawsul*) conveys the restriction (*qasr*) of the attribute of expelling those who disbelieved from their homes to God, Exalted is He. It is a restriction by claim (*qasr idde'i'i*), meaning that the efforts of the believers in that expulsion are not taken into account, and that they merely dealt with some of its causes, such as the destruction of the homes of the Banu al-Nadir.

[Page 66]

For this reason, the sentence ﴿you did not think they would leave﴾ serves as a justification (*ta'lil*) for the restrictive sentence.

The sentence ﴿and they thought that their fortresses would protect them﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) upon the cause, meaning: and they thought that the Muslims would not overcome them. The reason the text does not say "and they thought they would not be expelled" is that the discourse concerns their expulsion from the phrase ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved﴾. Instead, it moves to ﴿and they thought that their fortresses would protect them﴾, meaning, protect them from being expelled, dispensing with mentioning the object of the supposition by mentioning the cause of the supposition. The implied meaning is: "and they thought they would not leave, because their fortresses would protect them," that is, they thought strongly, relying upon their fortresses.

By ﴿those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is meant the Banu al-Nadir (pronounced *Nadir*, on the pattern of *Amir*), who were a tribe of Jews that settled in the lands of the Arabs, they and their cousins the Banu Qurayzah, and the Jews of Khaybar. All of them were descendants of Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him. The Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Qurayzah were called "the two priests" (*al-kahinan*), because each of these two groups descended from Harun, who was the priest of the Israelite community. *Kahanah* (priesthood) means the guardianship of the affairs of the religion in his hand and in the hands of his descendants.

The story of their settling in the lands of the Arabs is that Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, had sent a group of their forefathers to fight the Amalekites, who were neighbours of Syria and the land of the Arabs. They fell short in fighting them, and Musa died shortly afterwards. When they learned of Musa's death, they turned back on their heels to the lands of Israel in Jericho, and their people said to them: "You disobeyed the command of Musa, so do not enter our land." They therefore went out to the Arabian Peninsula and established for themselves villages around Yathrib (al-Madinah), and built for themselves fortresses and a village that they named al-Zuhrah. Their fortresses were five, whose names will be mentioned at the end of the commentary on this verse. They became people of crops and wealth. Among them were men of great wealth, such as Samaw'al ibn 'Adiya, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Ibn Abi al-Huqayq. Between them and the Aws and Khazraj there was an alliance and dealings. Among the branches of those Jews were the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah, and Khaybar.

They were labelled "those who disbelieved" because they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), as a branding upon them with this blameworthy attribute. They were described as "those who disbelieved" in His saying: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them, although before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], up to His saying "a humiliating punishment" in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 67]

On this basis, the particle *min* in ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*), because what is meant by the People of the Book here is specifically the Jews, that is, those who disbelieved in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). They are the People of the Book, and by them He means the Jews. They were described as "from among the People of the Book" so that it would not be thought that "those who disbelieved" meant the polytheists in Makkah or the remaining polytheists in Madinah, in which case it would be taken that the discourse was a threat.

The detailed account of the story to which the verse alludes, according to what the majority of the exegetes mention, is this: when the Muslims migrated to Madinah, the Banu al-Nadir came and made a treaty with the Prophet (ﷺ) that they would be neither against him nor with him. It is said that their treaty was after the battle of Badr, when the Muslims overcame the polytheists, because they had presumed that their banner would never be defeated. When the Muslims were defeated at the battle of Uhud, they broke their covenant and sought an alliance with the polytheists of Makkah, since they had held back from supporting them at the battle of Badr, in the manner of the Jews in allying with the strong. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who was the chief of the Banu al-Nadir, went out with forty riders, and they made an alliance with the polytheists at the Ka'bah, agreeing to be their helpers in fighting the Muslims. When this was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he commanded Muhammad ibn Maslamah to kill Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and he killed him by stealth in his fortress, in a story mentioned in the books of Sunnah and the biographies (*siyar*).

Ibn Ishaq mentions another cause: when the event of Bi'r Ma'unah ended in Safar of the fourth year (AH), 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri was a captive of the polytheists, and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl released him. When he was returning to Madinah, two men from the Banu 'Amir came, and their people had a covenant with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They stayed with 'Amr ibn Umayyah, and when they slept, he attacked them and killed them, thinking that he was avenging on the Banu 'Amir those who had killed the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Bi'r Ma'unah. When 'Amr ibn Umayyah arrived, he informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of what he had done. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "You have killed two men, and I shall pay their blood-money." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to the Banu al-Nadir, seeking their help in paying the blood-money for those two slain men, since there was an alliance between the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu 'Amir. The Banu al-Nadir secretly intended treachery against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but God informed him of it. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded the Muslims to prepare for war against them.

[Page 68]

Then the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Muslims to march against them in Rabi' al-Awwal in the fourth year of the Hijrah. He marched against them with the Muslims and commanded them to leave their village, but they refused and called to arms. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul secretly urged them not to leave their village, saying: "If the Muslims fight you, we will be with you and we will support you. If you are expelled, we will certainly leave with you." They therefore fortified the alleys, that is, they blocked the openings of some of them to others, so that each lane would be fit for defence, and they fortified them. He promised them that he had with him two thousand men from his people and others, and that with them were Qurayzah and their allies from Ghatafan among the Arabs. The Prophet (ﷺ) besieged them, and they waited for 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Qurayzah, and Ghatafan to come to them, to turn back the army of the Muslims from them. When they saw that these had not come to their aid, God cast terror into their hearts. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for peace, but he refused anything except their departure from their homes. They stipulated that they would leave, and that each three houses would carry a camel's load of whatever goods they wished from their property. They began to demolish their houses so that they could carry with them what they could benefit from, such as wood and doors.

They went out. Some of them joined Khaybar, and a few of them joined the lands of Syria, in the towns of Jericho and Adhri'at in the land of Syria. A few of them went out to al-Hirah.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿at the first gathering﴾ is the *lam* of time (*lam al-tawqit*), which is the one that enters upon the beginning of a time that is taken as an adverbial of time for an action, like His saying: ﴿He will say, "Would that I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], meaning "from the time of my life." And the saying: "He wrote for such-and-such a day." It has the meaning of *'inda* ("at"). The meaning is that He expelled them at the beginning of the gathering appointed for them. This is a hint that God decreed that they would leave all their homes in the lands of the Arabs. This decree was ordered by the Prophet (ﷺ), as will be mentioned later. Therefore, the definiteness of "the gathering" is definiteness by prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*).

*Hashr* (gathering) means assembling people in one place. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 36].

What is meant here is the gathering of the Jews of the Arabian Peninsula to another land, that is, their being assembled for departure. In this sense it is synonymous with *jala'* (exile), if the exile is of a large group gathered from the scattered lands of the country.

[Page 69]

What is not meant is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection, because there is no relevance to it here, and it does not suit the mention of the word "first," since the first of anything is necessarily of the same kind as that to which it is attributed.

It is reported from al-Hasan that he took the verse to refer to the gathering of the Resurrection, and people built upon that some illusions, supposing that the gathering of the Resurrection would take place in the land of Syria. It has already been mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas guarded against this when he named this surah "the Surah of the Banu al-Nadir." In making this expulsion the time of "the first gathering," there is an indication that their gathering would be successive until the expulsion of all the Jews is complete. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) recommended shortly before his death, when he said: "There shall not remain two religions in the Arabian Peninsula." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab carried this out when he expelled the Jews from all the lands of the Arabs.

It has also been said that the gathering was described as "first" because it was the first exile that befell the Banu al-Nadir. The Jews had been exiled from Palestine twice: once in the time of Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar), and once in the time of Titus, the Roman emperor. The Banu al-Nadir and those with them were spared from exile, because they were in the lands of the Arabs. Therefore, the first exile that befell them was the exile of the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from God.﴾

That is, the supposition of the Muslims and the supposition of the People of the Book converged on the impossibility of expelling the Banu al-Nadir from their village because of the strength of their fortresses.

The Jews used to build fortresses to which they retreated when the enemy attacked them, such as the fortresses of Khaybar.

The Banu al-Nadir had six fortresses, whose names are: al-Kutaybah (pronounced with *damm* on the *kaf* and *fath* on the *ta'* with two dots above), al-Watih (with *fath* on the *waw* and *kasr* on the *ta'*), al-Sulalim (with *damm* on the *sin*), al-Nata (with *fath* on the *nun* and *fath* on the *ta'* followed by an alif, and with the feminine ending at its end), al-Wakhdah (with *fath* on the *waw*, *sukun* on the *kha'*, which is dotted, and a *dal* which is undotted), and Shaqq (with *fath* on the *shin*, which is dotted, and a doubled *qaf*).

He composed the sentence ﴿and they thought that their fortresses would protect them﴾ in this arrangement, rather than saying "and they thought that their fortresses would protect them." The purpose is that it begins with their pronoun, since the predicate "protect them" (*mani'atuhum*) is then ascribed to it. Beginning with their pronoun indicates their being deceived by themselves, that they were in power and protection, and that the protection of their fortresses was among the matters of their might.

[Page 70]

As for placing "protecting them" (*mani'atuhum*), which is a descriptive noun, before "their fortresses" (*husunuhum*), which is a substantive noun, while outwardly the substantive is more appropriate to be placed in the position of the subject and the descriptive made a predicate about it, he departed from that to indicate the importance of the protection of the fortresses in their supposition. Thus it occupies the place of priority in bringing their supposition to mind. The permissibility of making "their fortresses" the agent of the active participle "protecting them" is disregarded, on the basis that it depends on a subject, since the meanings of eloquent speech follow the ways of disposing of the subtle meanings, so the permissible becomes less preferred.

Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on the chapter on *nasab* (genealogy/nisbah), concerning the verse of a poet, which is attributed to Dhu al-Rummah, but is not in the Diwan of al-Hamasah:

"If there is not but a brief pause of an hour, a little, then I am one who benefits from its little."

It is permissible that *qaliluha* ("its little") is the subject (*mubtada'*) and *nafi'un* ("one who benefits") is a predicate placed before it, that is, for the purpose of emphasis. The clause is in the position of the predicate of *inna*, and the meaning is: "Indeed I, its little is beneficial to me."

﴿So God came to them from where they did not expect, and He cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their homes with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take warning, O you with insight.﴾

Continuation of the commentary on the combined clauses ﴿so Allah came upon them from where they did not expect﴾ and ﴿they thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾, which together explain the restriction in His saying ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾.

The construction ﴿So Allah came upon them from where they did not expect﴾ is a figurative expression (tamthil, an illustrative image). It depicts the manner in which Allah facilitated their surrender after they had resolved to defend themselves, having both numbers and equipment, and their siege did not last long. It is like one who takes precautions against his enemy and tightly guards himself on every side, yet the enemy comes at him from a direction where he had posted no guard. This resembles the image in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

Al-ihtisab is an intensive form of al-husban, meaning al-zann (supposing or expecting). The meaning is "from a place they had not expected," because they had restricted their preparation to fortification and defensive strength, and did not know that the power of Allah is above their power.

[Page 71]

Al-qadhf means throwing with the hand with force. It is used figuratively for suddenly obtaining something, meaning that terror came into their hearts all at once, without prior reflection and without any apparent cause for terror. For this reason the verb of casting (qadhf) is not used in the verse of Al 'Imran: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 151].

The meaning is: Allah placed terror in their hearts, so they hastened to surrender. The casting of terror into their hearts is one of the circumstances of Allah's coming upon them from where they did not expect. Singling it out for mention is to express wonder at Allah's handiwork. Its coordination (ʿatf) with ﴿Allah came upon them from where they did not expect﴾ is coordination of the specific upon the general, for emphasis.

Al-ru'b is intense fear and dread. This is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been supported with terror," meaning with the terror of the enemies of the religion.

The clause ﴿they destroy their houses﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun attached to (qulubihim, "their hearts"), because the annexed noun is part of the annexed-to noun, and so this does not prevent the circumstantial clause from referring to it.

The intended meaning is to express wonder at the disorder of their affairs. Although they destroyed their own houses by their own choice, the motive for the destruction was compulsory.

Al-ikhrab and al-takhrib both mean the dismantling of a building and tearing it down. Al-kharab is the collapse of a building.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿yukhribuna﴾ with a sukun on the kha and a light ra with kasra, as the present tense of akhraba. Abu 'Amr alone read it with a fatha on the kha and a shadda on the kasra-ra, as the present tense of kharraba. Both have one meaning. Sibawayh said: af'ala and fa''ala interchange, as in akhrabtuhu and kharrabtuhu, and afrahtuhu and farrahtuhu, meaning in their basic sense. What was mentioned of the difference between anzala and nazzala has already been discussed in the first of the introductions to this tafsir.

The verse refers to what the Banu al-Nadir did to their own houses, dismantling them to take whatever could be used of timber and doors, which they carried with them to build their dwellings in their places of migration. It also refers to what the believers did to the remainder of those houses whenever they halted at a place, since the Banu al-Nadir had left them behind.

His saying ﴿by their own hands﴾ means their destruction of the houses with their own hands. It is literal regarding the act and what is connected to it. As for their destruction of their houses by the hands of the believers, it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), in which the destruction carried out by the believers is attributed to the Banu al-Nadir, on the basis that they caused the believers' destruction by leaving behind what they left.

So the phrase ﴿and the hands of the believers﴾ is coordinated with ﴿by their own hands﴾ in such a way that it becomes dependent on the verb ﴿yukhribuna﴾. This is a subtle usage, because the believers' destruction of the dwellings of the Banu al-Nadir, after finding them empty, is a true destruction to which the prepositional phrase truly attaches.

The meaning is: "They cause the ruin of their houses by the hands of the believers." Thus the attribution of the verb ﴿yukhribuna﴾ is literal, while the attachment of ﴿and the hands of the believers﴾ to it is on the basis of rational metaphor. The metaphor lies in the second attachment.

As for the meaning of destruction, it is literal with respect to both complements, since the literal meaning in both is the lesson pointed out by His saying ﴿So take warning, O you with vision﴾. That is, take warning from the fact that the destruction of their houses was by their own action, and the instruments of destruction were from their own equipment and that of their enemy.

Al-i'tibar is reflection on what things indicate concerning their implications, consequences and causes. It is an iftial form derived from al-'ibrah, which is admonition. The statement in the Qamus that al-'ibrah is "wonder" is deficient.

This was discussed earlier in the commentary on His saying ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111], in Surat Yusuf.

The address in His saying ﴿O you with vision﴾ is directed to an unspecified audience. The people of vision are called by this description in order to indicate that the lesson in the situation of the Banu al-Nadir is clear and manifest to every person of vision who witnessed it, and to every person of vision who sees the sites of their dwellings after them. For such a person, the lesson is the power of Allah to expel them and to give the Muslims power over them without fighting. It also lies in the triumph of truth over falsehood and the triumph of the people of certainty over the wavering.

Some scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) have used this verse as evidence for the authority of qiyas (analogical reasoning), on the basis that it is a form of i'tibar.

This is a tafsir passage, so I'll translate it in full.

Page 73

"Had it not been that Allah had decreed exile for them, He would surely have punished them in this world" (﴿Wa-law-lā an kataba Allāhu ʿalayhimu l-jalāʾa la-ʿaddhabahum fī l-dunyā﴾). This is a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtirāḍiyya) arising from the clause ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ (Q. 59:2). Thus the waw is the waw of parenthesis (wāw iʿtirāḍiyya), meaning: Allah expelled them from their town as a punishment for their disbelief and their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), as He said, ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ (Q. 59:4). And had Allah not punished them with exile, He would have punished them with killing and captivity, because they deserved punishment. Had He not cast terror into their hearts until they surrendered, He would have punished them with the hunger of the siege and conquered their homes by force, so they would have been punished with killing and captivity.

By "punishment" is meant the physical pain felt by the bodies, through killing, wounding, captivity and humiliation. Otherwise, expulsion from one's homeland is a calamity and a disaster, but it is not perceived by the senses; it is perceived only by the inner feeling (wijdān).

The particle (lawlā) is a particle of prohibition due to the existence of something (ḥarf imtināʿ li-wujūd), indicating that its response is prevented because of the existence of its condition. That is, the existence of Allah's decree of exile for them is the cause of the absence of Allah's punishing them in this world with another punishment.

Allah decreed exile for them rather than punishment in this world for a benefit required by His wisdom: that the Muslims would take their land, homes and orchards without the destruction of Muslim lives, which fighting does not avoid, because Allah willed to preserve the strength of the Muslims for the conquests to come. Thus the decree of exile for them was not for the purpose of showing them kindness and honour, even though they preferred it over war.

The meaning of (kataba Allāhu ʿalayhim) is: He decreed for them a decree, like writing in confirming its content. The manifestation of this divine decree was the calamities that followed them: the exile of the Naḍīr, then the conquest of Qurayẓa, then the conquest of Khaybar.

Al-jalāʾ is leaving one's homeland with the intention of not returning. Zuhayr said:

"Truly the right has three ends: an oath, or a fleeing, or an exile."

Know that the (an) that occurs after (lawlā) here is a verbal-masdar particle (maṣdariyya), because the (an) with a silent nūn, when it does not occur after a verb of certain knowledge or of supposition, nor after something that carries the meaning of speech, is a masdar particle and not a lightened form of the heavy (thaqīla) an.

"And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire" (﴿Wa-lahum fī l-ākhirati ʿadhābu l-nār﴾). This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Had it not been that Allah had decreed...﴾, or upon the clause ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved...﴾ (Q. 59:2) and what follows. It is not a conjunction upon the response of (lawlā), because the punishment of the Fire is certainly upon them and is not negated. The purpose is to guard against the supposition that exile is a substitute for the punishment of this world and for the punishment of the Hereafter.

The reference here is to everything mentioned: the expulsion of those who disbelieved from their homes, the casting of terror into their hearts, the ruin of their houses, and the preparation of punishment for them in the Hereafter.

The bāʾ is causal (*bāʾ al-sababiyyah*), and it governs the verbal noun formed from *an* (that) and its clause.

*Al-mushāqqah* (opposition, hostility) means enmity and hostility. Allah says: ﴿And He will say, "Where are My partners about whom you used to contend?"﴾ [al-Naḥl: 27]. Its counterpart was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Anfāl.

*Al-mushāqqah*, like *al-muḥāddah* (opposition), is derived from *al-shiqq* (the side or split), just as *al-muḥāddah* is derived from *al-ḥadd* (the limit), as was explained at the beginning of Surat al-Mujādilah. It was also mentioned in Surat al-Nisāʾ: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two of them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 35].

The Banū al-Naḍīr had declared enmity against the Muslims after they had settled in Madinah, harmed the hypocrites, and made alliances with the polytheists of Makkah, as you have learned a moment ago.

The clause ﴿And whoever opposes Allah, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is a concluding generalization (*tadhyīl*): that is, Allah is severe in punishment toward everyone who opposes Him, from these people and others.

Page 75

The name of the Messenger (ﷺ) is joined to the name of Allah in the first clause in order to magnify the Messenger's (ﷺ) status, so that they would know that obeying him is obedience to Allah, because he only calls to what Allah has commanded him to convey. The name of the Messenger (ﷺ) is not joined in the second clause, being sufficient by what is known from the first clause.

The two qāfs in *yushāqqi* are assimilated (*idghām*), because both assimilation and clarification (*izhār*) are permissible in Arabic in such cases. Both were read in His words: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] in Surat al-ʿUqūd. Unassimilated pronunciation (*fakk*) is the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and assimilation (*idghām*) is the dialect of the rest of the Arabs.

The clause ﴿then indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is the evidence for the answer to the conditional *man* (whoever). The implied meaning is: "And whoever opposes Allah, then Allah will punish them, indeed He is severe in punishment."

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down, or left standing on their roots, was by the permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), which leads to the surah's main theme: the rulings concerning the property of the Banu al-Nadir. The verse alludes to what happened during the siege of the Banu al-Nadir. Before they surrendered, they took refuge in their fortresses, and the Muslims besieged them. Their orchards lay outside their town, and the orchards were called al-Buwayra (pronounced with a short "u" and a long "u"; it is the diminutive of bu'r, with a hamza after the "b", which was softened into a "w"). Some Muslims set about cutting down some of the date palms of the Banu al-Nadir. It is said this was done on the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is said it was done without his command, but he did not forbid it to them. It is said that this was so they could clear space for their encampment, and it is said it was to frighten the Banu al-Nadir and to inflict harm on them. Some of the army refrained from cutting the palms and said: "Do not cut down anything of what Allah has granted us as spoils (fay')." It is mentioned that the palms that were cut down were six or two palms. The Jews then said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim to be a prophet who desires reform? Is it reform to cut down palms and burn trees? Did you find in what was revealed to you a permission for corruption on the earth?" So Allah revealed this verse.

The meaning is this: what they cut down of the palms was intended to serve the interest of forcing the enemy to surrender, of casting terror into their hearts, and of humbling them, by letting them see their most precious property exposed to destruction at the hands of the Muslims. What was left standing was not cut down, and its preservation served an interest, because it would ultimately belong to the Muslims as part of what Allah granted them. Thus there was an interest in both the cutting and the leaving standing, and the two interests conflicted. Allah's ruling was therefore to give the Muslims the choice. Dealing with the interests involved varies according to circumstances. Allah made both the cutting and the leaving standing "by His permission", that is, approved by Him. He used the word "permission" to mean approval, as a figure of speech (kinayah). Or He attributed the permission of Allah to the permission of His Messenger (ﷺ), if it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) first gave permission for this and then ordered them to stop.

The statements of the scholars are not clear about whether the Prophet (ﷺ) initially gave permission for it. The clearest of their views is that of Mujahid: the cutting and refraining from it was a point of disagreement among the Muslims, and the verse was revealed to confirm those who forbade cutting it down, and to declare lawful, with respect to sin, those who cut it. Concerning this, Hassan ibn Thabit said, mocking the polytheists in Mecca when the Muslims defeated the Banu al-Nadir, their allies, and mocking the Banu al-Nadir when their polytheist allies from Quraysh did not come to their aid:

"A group that supported Quraysh has been left without help, and they have no helper in their own land."

"And the blazing fire that spreads through al-Buwayra is held cheap by the chiefs of the Banu Lu'ayy ∗∗∗"

He means the nobles of the people of Mecca, all of whom are from the Banu Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib ibn Fihr, and Fihr is Quraysh. That is, they did not rescue their allies, because they held them in contempt.

Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who was then a polytheist, replied to him:

"May Allah keep such deeds going, and may the blaze burn in its surroundings."

"You will learn which of us will be unharmed by it, and you will learn which of our lands will be harmed."

He means that the burning took place in the areas around your city, so only your land is harmed, and our land is not harmed. So his saying "May Allah keep such deeds going" is sarcasm.

From this verse, the scholarly jurists who verify matters derived that burning and destroying the enemy's dwellings and cutting down their produce is permissible when a specific interest requires it. This is the view of Malik. Destroying part of one's property to save the rest is an interest.

His saying "of palms (min liyna)" is an explanation of what is meant by "whatever you cut down" (ma qata'tum).

Al-liyna is the palm that bears good fruit. The term liyna is applied to every palm other than the 'ajwa and the barnamiyy, according to the view of the majority of the people of Medina and of the leading lexicographers. The dates of the liyna are also called the "lawn" (al-lawn).

The choice of "liyna" over "nakhla" is because it is lighter (on the tongue). For this reason the word "nakhla" in the singular does not occur in the Qur'an; rather, "al-nakhl" occurs as a collective noun.

The lexicographers said: the "ya'" of liyna originally was a "waw", which became a "ya'" because it came after a kasra. They did not mention the reason for the kasra on its first letter. It is also said "lawna", and this is clear.

In the books of biography it is mentioned that some of the palms of the Banu al-Nadir were burned by the Muslims, and Hassan's poetry contains this. The Qur'an does not mention burning, so perhaps the report of burning was among the rumours that spread, and some narrators transmitted it, and it is reflected in the poetry of Hassan and in the poetry of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith. Or the palms that were cut down were burned by the army for cooking or for warmth.

The circumstantial phrase in His saying "standing on their roots" was brought to depict their form and beauty. In it there is a hint that leaving them uncut is preferable. The pronoun in "their roots" refers to "what" (ma) in His saying "whatever you cut down," because the meaning of "ma" here is plural, and it does not refer to "liyna", because the liyna does not have several roots; rather, each liyna has one root.

"On their roots" is connected to "standing". The purpose is to increase the depiction of its beauty. "Usul" means foundations. What is meant here is the trunk of the palm. He said: "Its root is firm and its branch is in the sky" [Ibrahim: 24]. Describing them as "standing on their roots" is with the implied sense: their branches standing on their roots, since it is evident that the root of the palm is part of it.

The "fa" in His saying "fa-bi-idhni Allah" (so by the permission of Allah) is extra, in the predicate of the subject, because the relative pronoun is a noun, and a relative pronoun is often treated like a conditional when it carries the sense of causation. It has been read both with "fa" and without it, as in His saying: "Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your hands have earned" [al-Shura: 30], in Surah al-Shura.

The conjunction in "and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient" is a conjunction of purpose (ta'lil) over cause, namely "fa-bi-idhni Allah", because the cause has the meaning of purpose. A parallel to it is His saying: "And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of Allah, and so that He might know the believers" [Al 'Imran: 166], in Al 'Imran.

[p. 78]

The meaning is: so the cutting of what you cut of the palms and the leaving of what you left were because Allah permitted the Muslims to do it for a benefit it held for them, "and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient," that is, so that He might humiliate the Banu al-Nadir, and they would see their precious property partly cut down and partly in the hands of their enemies. That is an honour for the believers and a disgrace for the disbelievers. The "defiantly disobedient" here refers specifically to the Jews of al-Nadir.

He turned away from using their pronoun, as was done with their pronouns before and after this verse, to referring to them by the description "defiantly disobedient", because a derived descriptive term indicates that the cause from which it is derived is the basis for the ruling. That is, He would disgrace them because of their defiant disobedience.

Fisq (defiant disobedience) means disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 6:

﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them—you did not spur horses or camels against it, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿whatever palm trees you cut down﴾ [al-Hashr: 5] and the rest of the verse, so that it is a favour (imtinan) and a completion of the expenditure of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir.

It is also permissible that it be a conjunction with the whole of what preceded it, the conjunction of one narrative to another narrative and one purpose to another purpose, for the transition to defining the fate of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir, so that the men of the Muslims would not differ over its division. And to clarify that what the Messenger (ﷺ) did in dividing the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was just, if the verse was revealed after the division. The referent of "what Allah restored" (mā afāʾa Allāh) is what they left behind of land, palm trees, building materials and wood.

Al-fayʾ (the spoils returned to the community) is a known term in the terminology of raiders. The verb afāʾa means "gave the fayʾ." Thus fayʾ in wars and raids is what the army gains of the enemy's goods, and it is more general than ghanima (booty). The lexicographers did not establish the original derivation, so fayʾ may come through fighting and may come without fighting, whereas ghanima is what is taken by fighting.

The pronoun in (minhum) refers back to those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, mentioned at the beginning of the surah, namely the Banu al-Nadir. It has been said that it refers to the disbelievers in general, and that it was revealed concerning the fayʾ of Fadak. This is far-fetched and contrary to the reports.

His saying ﴿so you did not spur against it﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of the relative pronoun (mā), joined with the fāʾ because the relative clause functions like a conditional, as it implies the sense of causation, as already mentioned just above in His saying "so by the permission of Allah."
By its explicit meaning it is a favour to the Muslims, in that Allah brought them the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir without fighting, like His saying, ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in battle﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25]. It also conveys, by way of implication (kināya), that by reporting that they did not spur against it, the intended necessary meaning of the statement is that they have no right of entitlement to it. The meaning: it is not of your right, or do not ask for its division, because you did not obtain it by your fighting, but Allah gave it to His Messenger (ﷺ) as a blessing from Him, without hardship or toil.

Al-ījāf is a kind of horses' movement: a swift pace with a rhythm, and it is meant as the galloping for a raid, because it is swift.

Al-rikāb is a collective noun for the camels that are ridden. The meaning: you did not raid against it with horses or camels.

The particle ʿalā in His saying ﴿so you did not spur against it﴾ indicates causation (ta'līl), and is not for making awjftum transitive, because the sense of ījāf does not govern fayʾ with a prepositional particle; or it is connected to an omitted element, namely the verbal noun of awjftum, i.e., "spurring for its sake."

The min in His saying "min khayl" ("with horses") is extra (zāʾida), entering on an indefinite noun in the context of negation, and what follows min is in the sense of the object of awjftum, i.e., "you did not drive horses or camels."

His saying ﴿but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾ is an exception (istidrāk) to the negation in His saying "so you did not spur against it," to remove the misconception that no one has a right to it. What is meant: Allah gave His Messenger (ﷺ) power over it, so the Messenger has the greater right to it. This construction conveys a semantic restriction (qaṣr maʿnawī), as if it were said: "Allah did not give you power over them, but He gave His Messenger (ﷺ) power over them."

In His saying ﴿but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾ there is concision by omission (ījāz ḥadhf), since the estimated meaning is: "but Allah gave His Messenger (ﷺ) power over them." And "Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills" stands in the position of a concluding generalization (tadhyīl) for its generality, and it indicates what is omitted.

Page 80
The generality of "whom He wills" includes that He gives His messengers power over combatants and gives them power over non-combatants.
The meaning: what Allah restored to His Messenger (ﷺ) is only by Allah's giving His Messenger (ﷺ) power, and by casting terror into their hearts, "and Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills." The concluding generalization thus dispenses with the omitted element, i.e., "you have no right to it, so it is from the wealth of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the rulers after him dispose of."

So the verse is an explanation of what took place in the division of the fayʾ of the Banu al-Nadir. For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not divide it among all the raiders, but divided it among the Muhajirun (Emigrants), whether they had fought with him or not, since the Muhajirun had no property. He wished to suffice them and suffice the Ansar with what they had given the Muhajirun of the palm trees. He gave the Ansar only three men from it, because of their great need: Abu Dujana (Simak ibn Kharasha), Sahl ibn Hunayf, and al-Harith ibn al-Simma. He gave Sa'd ibn Mu'adh the sword of Abu al-Huqayq. All of this was a disposition by the Messenger's (ﷺ) own judgment (ijtihad), because Allah had made that wealth his.

If the verse was revealed after the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir had been divided, it is an explanation that what the Messenger (ﷺ) did was right, which Allah commanded him to do or delegated to him. If it was revealed before the division, since it is reported that the reason for its revelation was that the army asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to take a fifth (takhmis) of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir, like the spoils of Badr, then this verse was revealed, and the verse was legislation establishing the entitlement to this wealth.

Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the first verse is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), i.e., this first of the two verses mentioned in this surah is specific to the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir, and that it is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who places it wherever he wills. In this view ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab spoke in the presence of ʿUthman, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, al-Zubayr and Sa'd, and it is the view of Malik as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb. He said: the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was pure (ṣāfiya) for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they agreed that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not take a fifth of it. Scholars differed over analogy (qiyas) to it: any wealth not obtained by spurring. Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

[Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on the verse, part 1]

﴿Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you﴾.

The majority of scholars treated this verse as the beginning of a new statement (ibtida' kalam), meaning a fresh resumption (al-isti'naf al-ibtida'i), and held that it was intended to convey a ruling different from the ruling contained in the preceding verse. Among these is Malik, and it is the view of the Hanafis. They took the content of the preceding verse to refer specifically to the property of the Banu al-Nadir, and they took this second verse as a report about the ruling on the fay' (property gained without battle) that was obtained when other towns were conquered after the expedition against the Banu al-Nadir, such as Qurayza in the fifth year and Fadak in the seventh year, and similar places. This verse therefore specified it for the categories mentioned in it, and no share in it belongs to the army either. This is what accords with the judgment of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in his ruling between al-'Abbas and 'Ali concerning the property of the Banu al-Nadir that was in their hands, though there is a possibility in that. It is also what the change in expression here requires: the words ﴿whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, after the previous verse said ﴿whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. The pronoun in "from them" refers to "those who disbelieved among the People of the Book," who are without doubt the Banu al-Nadir. On this view, this verse may have been revealed directly after the first verse, and it may also have been revealed after some time, since the conquest of the towns occurred about two years after the conquest of al-Nadir.

Some scholars took this verse as a continuation (kalimah) and an explanation (bayan) of the preceding verse, meaning an explanation of the general statement in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And you did not make any charge for it with horse or camel﴾ [al-Hashr: 6], and so on. This is because the preceding verse was limited to informing that the members of the army have no right to it, but it did not specify who is entitled to it. His words ﴿but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾ [al-Hashr: 6] indicated that it is property belonging to Allah, the Exalted, which He places wherever He wills through His Messenger (ﷺ). So Allah specified for him its rightful recipients from among those other than the army. Thus the position of this verse relative to the one before it is the position of explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan). For this reason it was separated (fusilat) from what precedes it.

Among those who held this view is al-Shafi'i, and the commentary of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) follows it. What this implies is [p. 83 ends here; continued below] that the property of the Banu al-Nadir was subject to the one-fifth division (takhmis), but no one has reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided it into fifths; rather, the opposite is established. On this view, the ruling on the property of the Banu al-Nadir is a special ruling, or else this verse abrogates (nasikhah) the preceding verse if it was revealed some time after it.

Ibn al-Faras said: The verse ﴿whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ is among the difficult verses when considered together with the preceding verse and with the verse on the spoils of war in Surat al-Anfal. There is no disagreement that His words, exalted is He, ﴿whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾ [al-Hashr: 6] and so on were revealed concerning what came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the property of the disbelievers without any charge of cavalry or camels, and 'Umar explained it this way and no one opposed him. As for the verse in al-Anfal, there is no disagreement that it was revealed concerning what came from the property of the disbelievers through charge and battle. As for the second verse of al-Hashr, the scholars differed about it. Some linked it to the one before it, and some linked it to the verse of al-Anfal, holding that the two were revealed with two different rulings concerning the spoils obtained through charge, and that the verse of al-Anfal abrogated the verse of al-Hashr.

Others said that it was revealed concerning a third meaning, other than the two meanings mentioned in the two verses. Those who held this differed: it was said that it was revealed concerning the kharaj (land tax) and the jizyah (poll tax) only, not the rest of the property; and it was said that it was revealed concerning the ruling on land alone, not the rest of the disbelievers' property. Thus it would be a specification (takhsis) of the verse of al-Anfal, and Malik adopted this view. According to those who hold this position, the verse is not abrogated. Others held that the imam has the choice (takhyir). End of quotation.

The definite article in His words, exalted is He, ﴿from the people of the towns﴾ (min ahl al-qura) is the definite of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and these are well-known towns. Among them are counted Qurayza, Fadak, the villages of 'Uraynah, Yanbu', Wadi al-Qura, and al-Safra', which were conquered in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). People differed over whether their conquest was by force ('anwatan), by agreed settlement (sulhan), or as fay'. Most hold that Fadak was like al-Nadir.

Making it belong to the Messenger is not restricted to the Messenger (ﷺ) himself; the leaders of the Muslims (a'immat al-muslimin) share in this in the same way.

Restricting the fay' to the fay' of towns follows what is usual, because usually only towns are conquered, since their people are besieged, surrender, and give in when the siege becomes severe. As for those who dwell in the desert, they are not overcome except after charge and fighting. Therefore the qualifier "from the people of the towns" has no implicit restrictive meaning (mafhum) in our view.

The jurists differed about the ruling on fay' that the Muslims obtain without charge. The position of Malik is that it is not divided into fifths; only the spoils (ghana'im), which are what the Muslims seize through charge and fighting, are divided into fifths.

Abu Hanifa adopted a distinction between movable property other than land and land itself. As for property other than land, it is divided into fifths. As for lands, the choice belongs to the imam according to what he sees as best: if he wills, he divides them and makes their people slaves (arqa'), and if he wills, he leaves their people in place and imposes kharaj on the land and on them.

Al-Shafi'i held that all property of war is divided into fifths, and he read the ruling of this verse in light of the ruling of the verse in Surat al-Anfal, either by specification or by abrogation.

This verse implies that a category of what Allah restored to the Muslims has no share given by Allah to the fighters. By this, a conflict arises between what this verse implies and the restriction in the verse of al-Anfal, which gave to those mentioned in this verse only the one-fifth. A group of scholars said: the verse of al-Anfal abrogated the ruling of this verse. Another group said: this verse abrogated the verse of al-Anfal. Qatada said: the spoils in the early period of Islam belonged to these five categories, and then this was abrogated by the verse of al-Anfal. Zayd ibn Ruman said this as well. Al-Qurtubi said: and something similar is reported from Malik. End of quotation. Moreover, Surat al-Anfal precedes Surat al-Hashr in revelation, because al-Anfal was revealed concerning the spoils of Badr, and Surat al-Hashr was revealed two years after it.

Unless someone says: the verse of al-Anfal was revealed after the verse of al-Hashr, renewing what Allah had prescribed concerning the division into fifths of the spoils of Badr. In that case the verse of al-Hashr would abrogate what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did in dividing the spoils of Badr, and then the verse of al-Anfal abrogated the verse of al-Hashr, so placing it alongside Surat al-Anfal would be by a directive from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Qurtubi said: It was said that Surat al-Hashr was revealed after al-Anfal, and they agreed that the division of spoils into fifths is what practice settled upon, by the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) and by consensus (ijma').

It is not far from my view that the towns which this verse refers to were conquered in a condition that was ambiguous between pure fay' and spoils (ghanimah), so a ruling specific to them was prescribed. Since their condition was not fixed, it was impossible to analogize from it, and its ruling was abrogated, and the matter settled on the limitation of conquests to two conditions: the condition of pure fay', and what is not pure fay'. The ruling of the verse of al-Hashr fell away through abrogation (naskh) or through consensus. Consensus that contradicts the ruling of a text is considered abrogating, because it implies an abrogating text. It is reported from Ma'mar that he said: It has reached me that this verse, namely "whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns," was revealed concerning the land of kharaj and jizyah.

Some scholars took it to refer to the land of the disbelievers when it is taken by force ('anwatan), such as the fertile land of Iraq (sawad al-'Iraq), but not the property of theirs other than land. All of this is confusion in reconciling this verse with the verse of Surat al-Anfal, even though the verse of al-Hashr precedes that one, together with what is reported from 'Umar in the case of his ruling between al-'Abbas and 'Ali, and with what 'Umar did concerning the fertile land of Iraq. You have understood the position of each. You will learn the reason for what 'Umar did concerning the fertile land of Iraq when speaking on His words, exalted is He, ﴿and those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr: 10].

Some scholars made the meaning of this verse cover all spoils, on the basis that they interpret fay' as synonymous with ghanimah. They claimed that it is abrogated by the verse of al-Anfal. What is meant by mentioning the name of Allah, exalted is He, among those who have the spoils and the fay', and the categories mentioned in this verse, has already been discussed, and their explanation was given earlier in Surat al-Anfal.

His words "so that it does not circulate" (kay la yakuna dulah) and so on are an explanation (ta'lil) of what the particle of possession (lam al-tamlik) implies, namely making it property of many categories of individuals. That is, We made it divided among these people so that the fay' does not become something circulating only among the rich Muslims, that is, so that the rich do not pass it among themselves and the needy receive no share of it.

What is intended by this is the nullification of what was customary among the Arabs before Islam: the leader of the army monopolizing certain parts of the spoils, namely: al-mirba' (a quarter), al-safaya (choice items), what was agreed upon by the enemy without fighting, al-nashitah (what the army seizes on its way), and al-fudul (the remainders).

['Abd Allah ibn Ghamma al-Dabbi said, addressing Bistam ibn Qays, chief of the Banu Shayban and their commander in their days:]

For you is the quarter of it, and the choice items, and your judgment, and the seized booty, and the surplus.

So al-mirba' is a quarter of the spoils, which the army's commander used to monopolize. Al-safaya are the precious items of the spoils that have no equal, so that dividing them is impossible, and the commander used to monopolize them. As for his judgment (hukm), it is what the enemy gave of property when they surrendered to the ruling of the commander of the army. Al-nashitah is what the army seizes of the property of its enemy on its way before it reaches the place of fighting. Al-fudul is what remains after dividing the spoils, of what does not accept division among the fighters, such as a camel or a horse.

Islam abolished all of that. It made the fay' spent on six channels of expenditure whose benefits return to the Muslims in general, to meet their general and particular needs. For what belongs to Allah and to the Messenger (ﷺ) is given by Allah for what His Messenger (ﷺ) commands, and He made the one-fifth of the spoils likewise for those same channels.

It has become clear from this reasoning that among the aims of the Shari'ah is that property should circulate among the Islamic community under a firm system in its transfer, from every property that no one previously owned, such as dead land (mawat), fay', lost items (luqatat), buried treasure (rikaz), or property that was a specific portion, such as zakat, expiations (kaffarat), the one-fifth of spoils, kharaj, and inheritances, and contracts of exchange that join property and labor, such as qiradh (profit-sharing), al-mughars (grafting), and musaqah (irrigation partnership); and in property that the one who gains it obtains without labor and effort, such as fay' and rikaz, and what the sea casts up. I have explained this in the book I named Maqasid al-Shari'ah al-Islamiyyah (The Objectives of Islamic Law).

Al-dawlah with a dammah on the dal means what is passed around by those who pass it among themselves. Al-tadawul means succession in handling something. Usage has restricted it to the circulation of property.

Al-dawlah with a fatah on the dal means a turn in victory and in ownership. For this reason the well-known readers (al-qurra' al-mashhurun) agreed on reading it with a dammah on the dal in this verse.

The majority read ﴿kay la yakuna dulah﴾ with "dulah" in the accusative as the predicate (khabar) of yakuna, and the subject (ism) of yakuna is a pronoun referring to "what Allah restored." Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with "dulatun" in the nominative, taking yakuna as a complete verb (tammah) and dulatun as its subject (fa'il).

The majority read yakun with a yā' at its beginning. Abu Ja'far read takun with a tā' at its beginning, following the feminine gender of its subject. The transmitters from Hisham differed: some of them transmitted from him agreement with Abu Ja'far on the tā' in takun, and some transmitted from him agreement with the majority on the yā'.

The address in His words, exalted is He, ﴿among the rich among you﴾ is to the Muslims, because they are the ones addressed at the beginning of the surah with His words ﴿You did not think that they would go forth﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], then His words ﴿What you cut of palm trees﴾ [al-Hashr: 5] and what follows it. Ibn 'Atiyyah made it an address to the Ansar, because the Muhajirun did not have wealth at that time.

The intended meaning of "the wealthy" (al-aghniya') is those who are the likely source of wealth (maẓẓat al-ghina), namely the warriors (al-ghuzat), because they are wealthy through the spoils of war (al-maghanim) and the battle gains (al-anfal).
