﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

This is an interjected sentence (i'tiraḍ) with which the ruling on the spoils of Banu al-Nadir (fay' Banu al-Nadir) is concluded, since it commands taking everything that the Messenger (ﷺ) brings, and among what these verses brought concerning the spoils of al-Nadir is [included]. The waw is an interjectory waw (waw i'tiraḍiyya). The purpose of this concluding sentence is to remove what was in the hearts of some of the army of a sense of resentment (ḥazazat) at being deprived of what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ) from the land of al-Nadir.

The word "giving" (al-itha') is used metaphorically for conveying the command to them: its legislation and its communication are treated as the giving of something into their hands, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. The word "taking" (al-akhdh) is also used metaphorically for accepting the command and being content with it.

The indication of this is its contrast with His words: ﴿and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾, and this completes the two kinds of legislation. This verse comprises the command to follow whatever proceeds from the Prophet (ﷺ) in word and deed, so all the proofs of the Sunnah (adillat al-sunnah) are included within it. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed... " — the hadith. This reached a woman of Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub, so she came to him and said: "It has reached me that you cursed such-and-such." He said to her: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah?" She said: "I have read what is between the two covers and I did not find in it what you say." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it. Did you not read: ﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?"

Following this command is a warning against opposition. He commanded them to fear Allah regarding what He commanded through the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Joining the command to fear Allah (al-taqwa) to the command to take the commands and abandon the prohibitions indicates that taqwa is the carrying out of the command and avoiding of the prohibition.

The meaning: "Fear the punishment of Allah, for Allah is severe in punishment," i.e., for whoever opposes His command and transgresses His prohibition.

﴿For the poor emigrants, who were expelled from their homes and their property, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾

It is a *badal* (substitution, or apposition) of what could be substituted for the preceding categories of recipients, whose names were directly preceded by the *lam* (the preposition meaning "for"). They are joined by the conjunction in His saying ﴿and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. It is a *badal ba'd min kull* (substitution of a part for a whole).

The first benefit of this substitution is to alert the reader that what Allah granted to the Muslims from the people of the towns referred to in the verse does not follow the same distribution as the property of the Banu al-Nadir, whose distribution was restricted to the emigrants, three men from the Ansar, and a fourth from among them. It is as though it were said: "For the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, namely, the poor among them, not absolutely, so that the emigrants, the Ansar, and those who came after them would be included."

The *lam* is repeated with the substitution to link it to the substituted term, because the separation between them is lengthened by intervening speech, including a reason (*ta'lil*), a concluding remark (*tadhyil*), and a warning (*tahdhir*), and also to add emphasis.

It is common for the substitution that governs the substituted term to occur in the manner of verbal emphasis (*ta'kid lafzi*). This was discussed in His saying ﴿It shall be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114] in the chapter al-'Uqud. There remains the possibility that it is a qualifier (*qayd*) of ﴿the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. In that case, His saying "for the poor" to the end must be understood as coming to restrict the entitlement of these categories. The rule regarding qualifiers that follow a series of nouns is that they apply to all that precedes them. This implies that poverty must be stipulated for each of these four categories, since their absolute form has been qualified by a qualifier following a series of absolutes. The context as a whole does not permit the dispute over applying the absolute (*mutlaq*) to the qualified (*muqayyad*) to arise, nor do the four cases of applying the absolute to the qualified apply, where the rulings and kinds of the two are the same. For this reason, Malik and Abu Hanifa said: the near of kin are given only if they are poor, because it is a compensation for them for what they were deprived of from zakat. Al-Shafi'i and many jurists said: poverty is stipulated for all except the near of kin, because it is their right by virtue of their kinship to the Prophet (ﷺ). Imam al-Haramayn said: al-Shafi'i sharply rejected the position of Abu Hanifa, saying that Allah linked the entitlement to kinship and did not stipulate need, so stipulating need and disregarding kinship harms and opposes it.

I say: this is the point of dispute, for Allah mentioned the description of orphans and of the wayfarer and did not stipulate need.

Imam al-Haramayn excused the Hanafis by saying that since charities were forbidden to the near of kin, the benefit of mentioning them in the one-fifth of the fay' and the spoils is that it is not prohibited to give it to them, just as charities are prohibited. Then he said: do not be deceived by the excuse, for the verse is explicit in establishing the entitlement as an honor for them; whoever explains it by need nullifies this meaning. End of quote.

Upon reflection, you will find that this rebuttal is flawed, and discussing it at length would be lengthy. Its proper place is the matters of jurisprudence (*fiqh*) and the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*).

Among the scholars and exegetes, some considered the clause ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ to be a new sentence (*jumla ibtida'iyya*) by omitting the subject. The implied meaning is: what Allah granted to His Messenger is for the poor emigrants, and so on to the end of what is conjoined to it. In this case, these are other channels for the fay'. Others considered it conjoined by omitting the conjunction, in the manner of enumeration, as though it were said: "So it is for Allah and for the Messenger," to the end, and then it was said: "for the poor emigrants." According to these two opinions, its being a qualifier of the preceding clause is negated, and other subtle points open up regarding applying the absolute to the qualified and the differences concerning the conditions for such application. These subtle points are clear to the careful reader. The first view is the one relied upon.

The emigrants were described as ﴿those who were expelled from their homes and their property﴾, to indicate that giving to them is intended to compensate for what they suffered in losing their property and homes, and that it also considers their sincerity in faith and that they repeatedly support the religion of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). He then concluded with His saying ﴿Those are the truthful﴾. The demonstrative ﴿those﴾ serves to honor their status and to alert that their deserving the description of the truthful is due to the attributes that preceded the demonstrative: that they were expelled from their homes and property, their seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and their support of Allah and His Messenger. For acts that are done purely for the sake of the One for whom they were performed bear witness to sincerity in them, through the hardships, harm, and injury that befall the doer. He could have escaped those hardships had he abandoned what he did for their sake or fallen short in it.

The sentence ﴿they are the truthful﴾ conveys restriction (*qasr*) through the pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*). It is a restriction by claim (*qasr idda'i*), for the sake of exaggeration in describing them with complete truthfulness, as though the truthfulness of others were not truthfulness in comparison with theirs.

The position of His saying ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ is like the position of His saying ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in the chapter al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And those who had already settled the abode and the faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and do not find in their breasts any need for what they have been given, and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves were in poverty. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul—it is those who are the successful.﴾

It is most apparent that (alladhīna, "those who") is conjoined to (al-muhājirīn), meaning: "and those who settled the abode."

Those who settled the abode are the Helpers (al-Anṣār).

The word ad-dār (the abode) is applied to lands, and its origin is the place of a tribe on the earth. It has also been applied to a town, as He, exalted is He, said concerning Thamud: ﴿So they were found in their homes, lifeless and prostrate﴾ [al-A'rāf: 78], meaning in their city, which is the Ḥijr of Thamud. The definiteness here is for a specific reference (al-'ahd), because what is meant by ad-dār is Yathrib, and the meaning is "those who are the people of the abode." This is a preparation for His saying: ﴿who love those who emigrate to them﴾.

At-tabawwu' (settling) is taking a mabā'a, which is the spot to which its owner returns (yabūʾu ilayhā), that is, returns to it after dispersing in his affairs. In the position of His saying (wal-īmān, "and the faith") there is an ambiguity, since it cannot validly be an object of the verb tabawwa'ū. The exegetes have interpreted it in two ways. One of them is that the speech be made a metaphor by implication (istiʿāra makniyya), by likening faith to a dwelling and making the attribution of settling an imaginative (takhyīl) device, so that the verb tabawwa'ū is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

The majority of exegetes have made the conjoined noun governed by a supposed verb indicated by the speech, its estimate being: "and they sincerely held the faith," in the manner of the words of the rājiz whose identity is unknown:
"I fed them chaff and cold water,"
and the words of ʿAbd Allāh ibn az-Zibaʿrā:
"Would that your husband had gone out, / girded with a sword and a spear,"
meaning: "and holding a spear." This is the view followed by az-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf). It has also been said that the waw is for accompaniment (lil-maʿiyya).

And al-īmān is an object with (maʿa) (maf'ūl maʿahu).

In my view this is the best of the interpretations, though few hold it. The majority treat the accusative on the object of accompaniment as merely transmitted from usage (samāʿī), so it is, in their view, rare in use, and they avoided deriving Qur'anic verses from it, to the point that Ibn Hishām in Mughnī al-Labīb claimed that it definitely does not occur in the Qur'an. And the interpretation of His saying ﴿So decide upon your affair, along with your partners﴾ [Yūnus: 71] is of this kind. This is because the Basrans stipulate that the governing element of the object of accompaniment must be the same as the governing element of the noun it accompanies, and they do not hold that the waw of accompaniment governs the object of accompaniment, contrary to the Kufans and al-Akhfash, for the waw in their view means "with" (maʿa). ʿAbd al-Qāhir said: it is accusative by the waw.

The truth is that there is no obligation that the object of accompaniment be governed by the verb. Do you not see the soundness of the speaker's saying: "The water and the wood leveled out" (istawā al-māʾu wal-khashaba), and their saying: "I traveled with the Nile" (sirtu wal-Nīl). And this conveys praise of them, that the abode of emigration is their abode, which they gave shelter to the emigrants, because it is the abode of believers, and nothing else at that time resembles it.

By this it becomes clear that the object of (min qablihim, "before them") is the verb tabawwa'ū alone, and that the prepositional phrase governed by it was restricted to it, not to anything mentioned after the waw, because the waw is not a conjunctive waw, and therefore it does not stand in place of the preceding verb, since the waw of accompaniment is in the sense of an adverbial of place (ẓarf), and so no prepositional phrase is attached to it.

In the mention of the abode, which is the city, together with the mention of faith, there is an allusion to the excellence of the city, in that their settling in the city is placed alongside praise of them for their faith. Perhaps this is what Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, meant in what Ibn Wahb narrated from him, who said: "I heard Mālik mention the excellence of Madīnah over other regions," and he said: "Indeed Madīnah was settled by faith and emigration, while other towns were conquered by the sword." Then he recited: ﴿And those who had already settled the abode and the faith before them love those who emigrate to them﴾, the verse.

The clause ﴿love those who emigrate to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from those who settled, and this is praise of them for what was established in their souls of the brotherhood of Islam, since they loved the emigrants. It is the habit of tribes to feel constrained by those who emigrate to their lands, because of the strain they impose.

Among the effects of this love is what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ concerning the report of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, when Saʿd offered him to share his property and to give up to him one of his two wives. They also housed the emigrants with them in their houses and granted them of their palm trees. And sufficient for you is the brotherhood which the Prophet ﷺ established between the emigrants and the Helpers.

His saying ﴿and do not find in their breasts any need for what they have been given﴾: "finding" is here used for mental perception, and the absence of finding a need is a metonymy for the absence of its existence, because if it existed they would perceive it in their souls. This is of the same kind as the words of the poet:
"And you do not see the lizard entering its hole therein."

Ḥāja (need), in origin, is the verbal noun of ḥawj, which is need, that is, dependence upon something. It is also applied to the thing needed, by the usage of the verbal noun for the passive participle. Here it is a metaphor for an aim and a purpose, and the application of need to an aim is a well-known metaphor which has come to be equal to the literal usage, as in His saying: ﴿and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾ [Ghāfir: 80], meaning that you may reach by them, in travel, the aim for which you travel; and His saying: ﴿except a need in the soul of Yaʿqūb, which he fulfilled﴾ [Yūsuf: 68], meaning an important purpose; and the words of al-Nābigha:
"Days when Nuʿm informs me, and I inform her / of what I conceal from people of my need and my secrets."

Accordingly, min in His saying mimmā ūtū ("for what they have been given") is then initial (ibtidāʾiyya), meaning: an aim or a desire arising from a booty (fayʾ) which the emigrants were given.

Ṣudūr (breasts) is meant here as the souls, the plural of ṣadr, which is the inner part in which the inner senses are located, and this is like the application of qalb (heart) to that.

What they have been given is the booty of Banū al-Naḍīr.

The pronoun in (ṣudūrihim) refers to those who settled the abode, and the pronoun in ūtū refers to those who emigrated to them, because "those who emigrated" is a group of the emigrants, so the pronoun is treated in accordance with the sense of min without its wording. These two pronouns, although they are third-person pronouns and are close to each other, the listener returns each pronoun to its referent according to the context, as in His saying: ﴿and they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [al-Rūm: 9] in Sūrat al-Rūm, and the words of ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās describing the victory of the Muslims with his people Banū Sulaym over Hawāzin:
"We returned, and had it not been for us, their host would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have secured what they had gathered,"
meaning that the army of Hawāzin secured what the army of the Muslims had gathered.

The meaning: that there does not stir in their souls any longing to take anything of what the emigrants were given from the booty of Banū al-Naḍīr.

Another possibility is that the word ḥāja be taken in its literal usage (the verbal noun of need, iḥtiyāj), since need in this sense can properly occur in the breasts, as it is among the emotional and affective states. The meaning of the negation of finding need in their breasts is that, because of their extreme love for the emigrants, it no longer occurs to their souls that they are in want of anything that the emigrants are given; that is, they are self-sufficient regarding what the emigrants are given, so their souls do not aspire to anything of what the emigrants are given, let alone seek it.

Min in His saying mimmā ūtū may be for causation (taʿlīl), meaning need for the sake of what the emigrants were given, or initial, meaning need arising from what the emigrants were given. Thus it conveys the negation of the finding of need in their souls and the negation of the causes of that finding and its usual sources among people, following rivalry and envy. The negation of the causes of need indicates the object of the omitted need, since the estimate is: "and they do not find in their souls any need for something that the emigrants were given."

Al-īthār (preference) is giving precedence to one thing over another by nobility or benefit.

The meaning: they prefer [others] over themselves in that, by their own choice, and this is higher in rank than what His saying ﴿and do not find in their breasts any need for what they have been given﴾ conveys; therefore it follows it, and the object of yu'thirūn is not mentioned, because His saying mimmā ūtū indicates it.

And among their preference for the emigrants is what is narrated in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "that the Prophet ﷺ called the Helpers to allot to them allotments of palm trees in Bahrain, and they said: No, unless you allot to our brothers among the emigrants the like of it."

As for the preference of one of them over another, there is what al-Bukhārī narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, hunger has afflicted me. He sent to his wives, but found nothing with them. The Prophet ﷺ said: Is there not a man who will host this one tonight? May Allah have mercy on him. A man from the Helpers, who was Abū Ṭalḥa, stood and said: I, O Messenger of Allah. He went to his household and said to his wife: This is the guest of the Messenger of Allah; do not withhold anything from him. She said: By Allah, I have nothing but the food of the children. He said: When the children want supper, put them to sleep, come and extinguish the lamp, and let us tie our bellies tonight. When the guest entered, and he [the host] made as if to eat, she got up to the lamp as if to fix it, and extinguished it, and showed him that we were eating. So they sat, and the guest ate."

Stories of this kind are mentioned in the exegeses. It has been said this verse was revealed concerning the story of Abū Ṭalḥa, and it has been said other than that.

The clause ﴿and even though they themselves were in poverty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The wāw is ṣilīyya (linking), and it is the one which indicates the mere conditioning of its answer upon a condition that conveys a state in which it is not thought that the answer occurs when that state occurs. The estimate: "even if they were in poverty, they would prefer [others] over themselves," so it is known that their preference in circumstances below that is all the more so, without conveying prevention. We have explained this at His saying ﴿So there will not be accepted from any of them the fill of the earth in gold, even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 91] in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

Al-khaṣāṣa: intensity of need.

The masculine form of the verb (kāna) is because the feminine of khaṣāṣa is not real, and because a prepositional phrase separates kāna from its subject. The bāʾ is for association (mulābasa).

The clause ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul—it is those who are the successful﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl), and the waw is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya), since, according to the correct view, a concluding clause is of the kind of parenthesis at the end of speech. The concluding of the speech by mentioning the excellence of those who are protected from the stinginess of their souls, after His saying ﴿and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves were in poverty﴾, indicates that their preference over themselves, even in a state of poverty, is a freedom from the stinginess of souls. It is as if it were said: because of their freedom from the stinginess of souls, ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul—it is those who are the successful.﴾

Shuḥḥ, with a ḍamma or kasra on the shīn, is an innate disposition in the soul to withhold what is its own, and it is close in meaning to miserliness (bukhl). Al-Ṭībī said: the distinction between shuḥḥ and bukhl is very difficult, and az-Zamakhsharī indicated the distinction between them in a way that implies that bukhl is the effect of shuḥḥ, namely that a person withholds what is asked of him to give. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the souls are made to be present with stinginess﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 128], meaning stinginess is made present with them and does not depart from them. It is attributed to the soul in this verse for this reason, so it is an innate disposition from which no soul is free.

In the ḥadīth explaining the best charity: "that you give in charity while you are healthy and stingy, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth." But souls differ in this measure. When it prevails over them in withholding what is good and beneficial, that is blameworthy, and its blame varies according to the variation of what it withholds. He said: One who has described it well is someone whose name I have not identified:
"He wrestles with a soul between his sides, rigid, / when he intends to do good, it says to him: Wait!"

So whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, that is, is protected from the blameworthy stinginess becoming a trait of his, because if he is protected from this trait he is safe from all the occasions of its blame. If he is protected from part of it, he has of success in proportion to what he was protected from.

The demonstrative is to magnify this category of people.

The form of restriction conveyed by the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is for emphasis, because of the abundance of success that follows from protection from the stinginess of the soul, so that it is as if the very class of the successful is restricted to that protected one.

Among the exegetes is one who made ﴿And those who had settled the abode﴾ the beginning of a new statement in praise of the Helpers (al-Ansar), in connection with the praise of the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). These ones did not give the Helpers any share in what Allah bestowed (afa') upon His Messenger from the people of the towns, and they restricted His saying ﴿what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ [al-Hashr: 7] to specific towns, namely: Qurayza, Fadak, Khaybar, al-Nafi', 'Urayna, and Wadi al-Qura. They also related that "when Allah bestowed upon His Messenger ﷺ the fay' of these, he said to the Helpers: 'If you wish, I will divide with the Emigrants from your properties and your homes, and you will share with them in this spoil; and if you wish, you may keep your properties and leave these to them.' They said: 'Rather, we will divide our properties with them and leave this spoil to them.' So the verse ﴿what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ [al-Hashr: 7] was revealed," and so on.

Among them is one who restricted this verse to the fay' of the Banu al-Nadir. All of this is a departure from the established course of the verses of this surah in their coherence with one another, and a dismantling of the structure and harmony of the discourse, together with the weakness of the reports they related concerning it. Therefore, reliance upon it is not appropriate. According to this interpretation, the conjunction of ﴿And those who had settled the abode﴾ is a conjunction of one clause upon another clause, with the relative pronoun as the subject (mubtada') and the clause ﴿they love those who emigrate to them﴾ as the predicate (khabar) of the subject.

[p. 96]

It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿those who settled in the abode﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], according to the two interpretations mentioned above. As for the view of those who made ﴿those who settled in the abode﴾ [al-Hashr: 9] conjoined to "for the poor emigrants" (lil-fuqarāʾ al-muhājirīn), they made ﴿those who came after them﴾ a group from the people of the towns (ahl al-qurā), who are other than the emigrants and the Helpers (al-anṣār). Rather, they are those who came to Islam after the emigrants and the Helpers. So the pronoun in "after them" (min baʿdihim) refers to the two groups together.

The verb "came" (jāʾū) is used to mean arriving at, and coming to, a state that resembles their state, which is the state of Islam. It is as if they came to a place to settle there. This is a third group. These are the ones mentioned in His saying, after the mention of the emigrants and the Helpers, ﴿and those who followed them in goodness﴾ [al-Tawba: 100], that is, who followed them in faith.

The verb "came" (jāʾū) was phrased in the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) by way of prevalence (taghlīb), because among the Arabs and others there were those who embraced Islam after the Hijra, such as the tribes of Ghifār, Muzayna and Aslam, and such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and Salmān al-Fārisī. It is as if it were said: "those who came and those who will come," by the indication of the implicit sense of the discourse (lahn al-khiṭāb). The purpose of this is to add a further removal of the impression that the emigrants alone should be singled out for what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger ﷺ from the people of the towns, just as the Prophet ﷺ singled them out with the fay' (spoils acquired without fighting) of the Banū al-Naḍīr.

This verse includes every Muslim who exists until the end of time, and upon this was the understanding of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu). Al-Bukhārī reported through the chain of Mālik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar said: 'Were it not for the last of the Muslims, no town would be conquered but that I would divide it among its people (that is, the conquerors), as the Prophet ﷺ divided Khaybar.'"

Al-Qurṭubī mentioned that ʿUmar gathered the emigrants and the Helpers, consulted them about what Allah had bestowed upon him, and said to them: "Consider the matter and reflect upon it, then come to me in the morning." When they came to him in the morning, he said: "I have passed over the verses which are in Sūrat al-Ḥashr," and he recited ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 7], up to His saying ﴿those are the truthful﴾. He said: "They are not only for these (people)." Then he recited ﴿And those who came after them﴾ up to His saying ﴿Compassionate and Merciful﴾. Then he said: "No one remains among the people of Islam but that he has entered into this." End of quotation.

This is evident regarding the fay'. As for what was conquered by force (ʿanwatan), that is a separate question, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb had another ruling concerning his not dividing the land of Sawād of Iraq among the army of the conquerors. That is not our aim here, and its place is in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh) and hadith.

As for the group of the exegetes (mufassirīn) who made His saying ﴿and those who settled in the abode and in faith﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 9] a new independent statement, and made ﴿who love those who emigrate to them﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 9] the predicate of the relative pronoun, they also made His saying ﴿and those who came after them﴾ an independent statement in the same way.

Among those who made His saying "and those who settled" conjoined to ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 8] is the one who made His saying ﴿and those who came after them﴾ an independent statement. Ibn al-Faras attributed this in Aḥkām al-Qurʾān to al-Shāfiʿī, and he held that the fay', when it is land, is at the discretion of the Imam, and it is not necessarily restricted to the categories mentioned in the fay' of the Banū al-Naḍīr.

The clause ﴿they say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾, according to the preferred interpretation, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿those who came after them﴾.

Ghill (rancour), with a kasra on the ghayn, is envy and hatred. That is, they asked Allah to purify their souls from rancour and envy toward the believers who preceded them, because of what those were granted of the virtue of companionship with the Prophet ﷺ, and what some of them were distinguished by in emigration and others by support. Then Allah made clear to those who came after them what would earn them a virtue that the emigrants and the Helpers do not have, namely the virtue of praying for them for forgiveness, and their inner hearts being folded over love for them, and the absence of hatred toward them.

What is meant is that they conceal in their souls what they ask Allah on their behalf, and they are content with themselves upon it.

The verse indicates that it is a right upon the Muslims to remember their predecessors with good, and that it is a right upon them to love the emigrants and the Helpers and to honour them. Mālik said: "Whoever hates any of the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ, or has rancour in his heart toward them, has no right to the fay' of the Muslims." Then he recited ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse.

Perhaps he took this from the implicit meaning (mafhūm) of the circumstantial clause in His saying ﴿they say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾, the verse, for the purpose of praising them with this is that they conceal its content within their souls. So when they conceal the opposite and openly declare what contradicts that, this attribute has failed to be present in them. The fay' is a gift which Allah bestowed upon those categories, and they did not acquire it by right of fighting. Therefore Allah made it a condition for their entitlement to it that they be lovers of their predecessors, not envious of them.

[p. 98]

This means: except for enmity that arises between two persons for customary or legal reasons, such as what occurred between al-ʿAbbās and ʿAlī when they brought their dispute before ʿUmar, and al-ʿAbbās said: "Judge between me and this wrongdoer, treacherous, deceitful one." And such as ʿUmar's enforcement of the penalty for slander (ḥadd al-qadhf) upon Abū Bakra.

As for what took place between ʿĀʾisha and ʿAlī of dispute and fighting, and between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya of fighting, it was only the support of truth according to the view of each of the two sides, and it was not due to rancour or belittling. It is like a judge's striking someone for the purpose of discipline. Therefore it is obligatory to refrain from partisanship toward them, or toward others, after them. For although that may be permissible for individuals because their ranks are equal or close to each other, the presumption about them is that the resentments were removed from their hearts when those events ended. It does not permit this for the followers after them, who are not among them, being neither in the caravan nor in the raiding party. Rather, it is only a trace of the zeal of the Jāhiliyya (Age of Ignorance) which gnawed at the strength of the Muḥammadan community.

﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite, saying to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you." And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾.

He follows his mention of what befell Banu al-Nadir and what is connected to it, with an explanation of its causes, and then with an explanation of how their spoils (fay') and the spoils of the towns conquered after that are to be distributed. He mentions the state of the hypocrites with Banu al-Nadir and how they deceived them with false promises, so that the Muslims would know that hypocrisy is a disposition in those people that they do not abandon, even when they are on the side of a people whom they wish to prevail over the Muslims.

The sentence is a fresh resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins an independent statement). The interrogative is used to express wonder at the state of the hypocrites. It is built upon the negation of knowledge of their state, as a metonymy (kinayah) that urges one to attain this knowledge, as if he is saying: "Consider those who played the hypocrite in the state of their speech to their brothers, and do not stop looking into that, for it is a strange state." The detailed meaning of the phrase "Have you not considered such-and-such" (alam tara ila kadha) has already been explained at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 99]

The clause "yaqulun" (they say) is in the position of the second object. The estimated sense is: "Have you not seen them saying?" The present tense is used to convey that this was repeated from them, meaning they say it insistently, emphasizing it and repeating it, not as a matter of bada' (a change of mind that appears suddenly, a new opinion that arises) or a passing thought that was set aside.

The ones referred to by "those who played the hypocrite" here are a group of Banu 'Awf from the Khazraj among the hypocrites. Named among them are 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, 'Abdullah ibn Nabtal, Rifa'ah ibn Zayd, Rafi'ah ibn Tabut, Aws ibn Qayzi, Wadi'ah ibn Abi Qawtal or Ibn Qawqal, Suwayd, whose lineage is not recorded, and Da'is, whose lineage is not recorded. They sent to Banu al-Nadir when the army of the Muslims besieged Banu al-Nadir, saying to them: "Stand firm in your strongholds, for we are with you."

By "their brothers" is meant Banu al-Nadir. He described them as brothers to them only because they were united in disbelief in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is not brotherhood of lineage, for Banu al-Nadir were Jews, while the hypocrites who sent to them from Banu 'Awf were Arabs of Madinah, and their origin was from al-Azd.

In describing their brothers as "those who disbelieved" there is an indication that the bond of brotherhood between them is disbelief, although the disbelief of the hypocrites is the disbelief of polytheism (shirk), and the disbelief of their brothers is the disbelief of the People of the Book, which is disbelief in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The lam in "la-in ukhrijtum" (if you are expelled) is an introductory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah) preparing for an oath; that is, they said to them a statement emphasized with an oath.

They promised them that they would go out with them only so that they would feel secure about their support, so this is a metonymy for support. Otherwise, they would not agree to leave their lands.

The clause ﴿and we will never obey anyone concerning you﴾ is conjoined to the clause "if you are expelled," so it is part of what is said, not part of what is sworn to. It is left without emphasis, because Banu al-Nadir know that the hypocrites do not obey the Messenger (ﷺ) or the Muslims, so the hypocrites had no need to affirm this report.

The meaning of "concerning you" (fikum) is "regarding your affair," which is known from the context. That is, "in your harm," since it does not occur to the mind that they would not obey whoever calls them to allying with their brothers. The omitted noun in such a case is estimated according to what suits the context. A parallel to this is His, exalted is He, saying ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is disease hastening toward them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52],

[Page 100]

meaning: in allying with them. The meaning of "we will surely support you" (lananṣurannakum) is "we will surely help you in fighting." The word "nasr" (support) is applied to aid against an enemy. Allah informed His Messenger (ﷺ) that they were liars in that, after He had informed him of what they swore to, to reassure his heart. This is because the verse was revealed after the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir and before the raid on Quraydhah, so that the Messenger (ﷺ) would not be apprehensive out of fear of the might of the hypocrites. Allah called the report "testimony" (shahadah) because it is a report from certainty, in the position of testimony, about which the one who reports does not speak recklessly.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 12:

﴿Even if they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and even if they are fought, they will not help them.﴾

An explanation (bayan) of the sentence ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ [al-Hashr: 11].

The lam is a lam of preparation (muwatti'ah) for the oath (qasam), and this is a confirmation from Allah Most High to His Messenger (ﷺ) that they will never harm him in any way, so that he does not pay heed to what has reached him of their speech.

The pronoun in (ukhrijū) and (qutilū) refers to those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, that is, those who had not gone out and had not yet been fought, namely the Banu Qurayza and Khaybar. As for the Banu al-Nadir, they were expelled before the revelation of this surah, so they are not intended by this future report. The meaning is: if the remainder of the Jews are expelled in the future, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought in the future, they will not help them. He has taken the path of elaboration (itnab) in this explanation, for His saying ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ [al-Hashr: 11] contained what is in these two sentences, so its explanation came by way of elaboration to increase the affirmation of their lying.

* * *

﴿And even if they help them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped.﴾

This is an ascent (irtiqa') in refuting them regarding what they promised their brothers. The waw is the waw of the circumstantial clause (wawu al-hal), not the waw of conjunction (wawu al-'atf).

The verb (nasarūhum) means the intention of the act's occurrence, indicated by His saying ﴿they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped﴾. So the use of the verb to mean its intention is like His Most High saying ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], the verse [continues]

Page 101

and His saying ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and His Most High saying ﴿For those who swear off their wives, a waiting period of four months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], meaning: those who intend to return to what they refrained from by the oath of abstention (iyla'). The meaning is: even if it is supposed that they intended to help them, such people are not expected to be steadfast in the battle, so if they intended to help them and prepared with them, they would flee at the moment of terror. This is like His saying ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing but corruption to you, and they would have hurried between your ranks﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47].

It is also permissible that (nasr) was used for assistance with men and equipment, which is among the meanings of nasr.

The (thumma) in His saying (thumma la yunsarun) is for delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usual function in conjoining sentences, for the non-existence of victory is of greater rank in despairing the People of the Book of benefiting from the aid of the hypocrites, so it is stronger than the defeat of the hypocrites when they come to aid the People of the Book in fighting.

The nasr here means: victory (al-ghalab).

The pronoun in (la yunsarun) refers to those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, since the discourse runs on the promise of the hypocrites to help the People of the Book.

The purpose is to strengthen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims and to secure them from the might of their enemies.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾

Since the purpose of mentioning the weakness of the hypocrites in fighting was to strengthen the resolve of the Prophet ﷺ and of the believers, so that they would not fear them or dread their support for the enemies of the Muslims, the allies of the hypocrites, Qurayzah and Khaybar, it follows this with informing the believers that the hypocrites and their allies fear the Muslims with a severe fear. The intensity of this fear is described as being greater than their fear of Allah, Exalted is He, for the fear of all creation of Allah is greater. So when fear in someone's heart reaches the point of being greater than the fear of Allah, that is the extreme of fear.

The purpose is to reinforce the souls of the Muslims so that they know that their enemy is terrified of them, and this increases the Muslims in boldness in fighting them. The context of the speech is not to record against the hypocrites and the Jews their lack of fear of Allah, but rather to inform the Muslims that they are more terrifying to them than every greatest terror.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and those with him among the Muslims.

By "breasts" (ṣudūr) is meant the souls and the consciences, because the locus of their faculties is in the breasts.

Al-rahbah (dread) is the verbal noun of rahiba, meaning he feared.

His saying "in their breasts" relates to "rahbah," so it is their dread.

The pronoun in "their breasts" refers to those who hypocritically professed faith and "those who disbelieved among the People of the Book," since neither of the two groups' name is more deserving of the return of the pronoun to it, given that the pronoun is suitable for both of them. Also, because the ones targeted by fighting are the Jews of Qurayzah and Khaybar, while the hypocrites were their helpers.

The attribution of "more intense" (ashadd) to the pronoun of the addressed Muslims is a causal attribution, as if it were said: "Your dread in their breasts is more intense than a dread in them." So "rahbah" carries the meaning of a verbal noun attributed to its object, and every verbal noun of a transitive verb may be attributed to its agent or to its object. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it as "more intense in being feared" (ashadd marhūbiyyah).

"Min Allah" is the element of comparison, and it is by elision of an annexed term, meaning "than the dread of Allah," i.e., than their fearing Allah, as al-Nabighah said:

"I have feared so much that my fear does not exceed
the fear of a wild goat on the mountain of al-Mutarah, one who is sensible."

That is, beyond the fear of a wild goat.

This is a structure, strange in its composition and wondrous in its style. The customary way of expressing this meaning would be to say: "Indeed their dread of you in their breasts is more intense than their dread of Allah," but it was turned away from this composition to the composition in which it was framed in the verse, so that the beginning could be with the pronoun of the Muslims, giving it importance, and so that the object of the dread would be the very persons of the Muslims, anticipating their striking, and so that the specification (tamyīz) transferred from the subject would come, for what it contains of the peculiarity of summary together with detail, as has been established in the peculiarity of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿واشتعل الرأس شيبا﴾ [Maryam: 4] rather than "and the whiteness of my head ignited." And so that the elision of the annexed term could occur in the phrase "min Allah," since the estimate is "from the dread of Allah," because its elision is not good except when its position is connected to the word rahbah; it is not good to say: "Their dread is more intense than Allah." Refer to what preceded at the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إذا فريق منهم يخشون الناس كخشية الله أو أشد خشية﴾ [al-Nisa': 77] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The Jews and the hypocrites, by their nature, ought to fear Allah. As for the Jews, they are people of a religion, so they fear Allah and beware of the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. As for the hypocrites, they are polytheists, and they acknowledge that Allah, Exalted is He, is the Greatest God, and that He is most deserving of being feared, since He is the Lord of all, but they do not affirm the Resurrection and the recompense, so their fear of Allah is restricted to fear of the punishment of this world, such as being swallowed up by the earth, drought, annihilation, and the like, and there is no fear beyond that. This is good news for the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims, that Allah has cast terror of them into the hearts of their enemies, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "I have been supported with terror across a distance of a month's journey."

As for describing the dread as being "in their breasts," it indicates that it is a very hidden dread, i.e., they pretend to be prepared for fighting the Muslims and display boldness so that the Muslims will dread them, while they are not in that position. So Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of their inner state, and therefore His saying "in their breasts" is not a revealing description.

Since the good news has been established from the report about the terror that is in their hearts, the discourse turns to censure of these enemies because of their being more fearful of people than of Allah, Exalted is He, that this is due to a deficiency in the understanding of their souls. Had they understood, they would have been more fearful of Allah than of people, so they would have considered what would save them from the punishment of neglecting consideration of the call of the Messenger ﷺ, and they would have known his truthfulness, and thus been saved from the consequences of their disbelief in him in this world and the Hereafter. Their dread of the Muslims would then have been a calamity upon them and a benefit to the Muslims.

Thus the sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the explanation and what it explains.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than Allah﴾. The bringing of the demonstrative is so that the matter judged upon is distinguished with the utmost distinction, because of its strangeness.

The "bi" (ba') is causal, and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the demonstrative, meaning: the cause of that mentioned matter is the absence of their understanding.

The inclusion of the word "people" (qawm) indicates that the lack of understanding of their souls is a matter by which they are all known and has become one of the constituents of their peoplehood, such that none of them is free of it. Its explanation has already been given at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of night and day﴾ [Yunus: 6] through to ﴿surely there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Fiqh (understanding) is comprehension of hidden meanings. It has already been explained at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ [al-Nisa': 78] in Surat al-Nisa', and His saying: ﴿See how We vary the signs that perhaps they may understand﴾ [al-An'am: 65] in Surat al-An'am. That is because they followed the motives of visible fear and were oblivious to the fear that is hidden from their sight, which is the fear of Allah. So that was due to their lack of understanding of hidden things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 14:

﴿They will not fight you all together, except in fortified towns or from behind walls.﴾

This clause is a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute clause that is included in the meaning of what precedes it) for the clause ﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 13], because the intensity of fear of the Muslims includes the intensity of seeking fortification against fighting them. That is, they are not able to fight you except in these conditions. The pronoun in *yuqatilunakum* ("they fight you") refers to those who disbelieved among the People of the Book.

His saying *jami'an* ("all together") may mean "all of them," as in His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. In this case it is for comprehensiveness, meaning: all of them, the Jews and the hypocrites, do not fight you except in fortified towns, etc.

It may also mean "gathered together," meaning: they do not fight you as armies, as is the case with the armies of allies, for that is the fighting of those who do not remain in their villages. In this case the negation is directed at this restriction, meaning: they do not gather together to fight you as armies do. That is, they do not attack you, but they fight a defensive battle in their villages.

The exception "except in towns" according to the first reading of *jami'an* is a *istithna' haqiqi* (a genuine exception) from the generality of circumstances, meaning: they do not fight you all together in any circumstance except in the circumstance of being in fortified towns, etc. According to the second reading of *jami'an*, it is a *istithna' munqati'* (a disjunct exception), because fighting in towns and from behind walls is not one of the circumstances of fighting of armies that support one another.

On both possibilities, the restriction indicates that they fight only in a scattered way, each group in its own town, and only while fearful and sheltered behind defences.

The meaning is: they do not attack you, and if you attack them, they do not come out to face you, but they defend themselves in fortified towns or fight you from behind walls, that is, in fortresses, strongholds and behind ramparts. This is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for their ending in defeat, since no people are fought in the heart of their homes without being humiliated, as 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said. This is an informing to them, and a reassurance to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, and an exposing of the hidden intentions of the enemies.

The word *judur* with two *damma*s, in the recitation of the majority (*al-Jumhur*), is the plural of *jidar* (wall). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited it as *jidar* (singular), and the intended meaning is the genus, which is equivalent to the plural.

And *muhassanah* means: protected from those who wish to take them, with ramparts or trenches.

*Qura* is with the short vowel pattern (*al-qasr*), the plural of *qaryah* (town). Its form and its being shortened is irregular, because what is in the pattern *fa'lah* with a weak final radical, like *qaryah*, is pluralized as *fi'al* with a kasra on the first letter and with a long vowel, as in *rakwah* / *rika'* and *shakwah* / *shika'*. The shortened form has only been heard in *kawwah* (opening, niche), with a fatha on the kaf, in the plural *kuwa*, and *qaryah* / *qura*. For this reason al-Farra' said: "*Qura* is anomalous," meaning, it departs from the rule.

* * *

﴿Their might among themselves is severe. You think them to be together, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

This is a *isti'naf bayani* (an explanatory resumptive clause), because the information about the People of the Book and their supporters, that they do not fight the Muslims except in fortified towns, implies that they do not unite in a single army supporting one another. This prompts the hearer to ask about the reason for this, even though they are united in enmity against the Muslims. So it is answered that among them there is severe might and mutual hostility, so they do not unite.

The clause opens with *ba'suhum* ("their might") to emphasise the information about it, that it is "among them," that is, it is exercised by some of them over others, and their might is not against the Muslims. This also contains a note of mockery.

The meaning of "among them" is that the field of might is within their own circle, so whatever harm their might causes is reflected back upon them. This structure is like His saying: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

The clause ﴿You think them to be together﴾ to its end is a resumptive clause after the clause ﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾. This is because the questioner may ask: how is that, when we see them united? So the answer is that the outward state of their condition is one of gathering and unity, while inwardly they are divided. Their opinions do not agree, and there is no affection between them, because among them are rancour and enmities, so they do not support one another.

The address is to an unspecified audience, because the Prophet ﷺ would not think this. This is an encouragement for the Muslims to fight them and to look down on their group. In the verse there is also an education for the Muslims, so that they beware of disagreement and mutual hostility, and know that the community cannot be formidable to its enemies unless its hearts are in agreement, holding a unified view on the fundamental principles of their shared interests, even if they differ in particular matters that do not violate the fundamental principles of their interests and do not split their unity. Also, unity is not achieved by agreement in words, nor by agreement on aims, unless the hearts are pure of rancour and enmity.

*Al-qulub* ("the hearts") means the minds and opinions, and applying the word "heart" to the intellect is common in the language.

*Shatta* is the plural of *shatit*, meaning "separated," in the pattern *fa'la*, like *qatil* and *qatla*. The minds whose aims differ are likened to groups scattered in different directions, in that they do not meet in one place. The meaning is: they do not agree to wage war against the Muslims.

His saying *dhalika* ("that") refers to what was mentioned: that their might is among themselves and that their hearts are scattered. That is, this is caused by their lack of reason, as they were driven to satisfy the impulses of grudges and to take vengeance among themselves, and neglected to consider the outcomes of affairs and to follow what is beneficial, so they wasted the interests of their own people.

[Page 107]

For this reason the word *qawm* ("a people") was inserted in His saying ﴿because they are a people who do not reason﴾, to indicate that this comes from the weakness of their minds, to the point that their minds are as if nonexistent. So the meaning is: they do not reason with sound reasoning.

Here ﴿do not reason﴾ (*la ya'qilun*) is chosen, while in the verse before it, ﴿do not understand﴾ (*la yafqahun*) is used. This is because knowing the outcome of scattering in opinion, and of turning might against a partner in shared interest, which brings weakness and erosion to the arm of the community, is a knowledge that is *mashhurah* ("well known") among the wise. A man of the Banu Nabhan, addressing his people when they had resolved to fight one another, said:

*And indeed, prudence is that you should not turn the points of your spears toward a tribe other than us.*

So their neglect of this conduct made them equal to those who have no reason, and this condition was a wretchedness for them, from which came happiness for the Muslims.

It has been mentioned more than once before that attributing a judgment to the title of a people indicates that this judgment is like an innate nature that constitutes that people's character, and I have mentioned it just now.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 15:

﴿Like those before them who had recently tasted the evil consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

It is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), indicated by this predicate. The construction is: "Their situation is like the situation of those before them, recently," i.e., the condition of the People of the Book who were promised support by the hypocrites is like the condition of those who were before them recently.

What is meant is that their condition is composed of displaying strength while concealing fear of the Muslims; of division between them and their fellow People of the Book; of the hypocrites forsaking them when they are in need; and of their fighting the Muslims only from fortified towns or from behind walls. This is like the condition of those who were before them in a recent time, namely the Banu al-Nadir, who showed readiness for war and refused to leave (al-jala'), so they did not fight except in their town, having fortified it and remained within it until the siege wore them down, and they were compelled to leave. The hypocrites did not benefit them, nor did their brethren among the People of the Book.

And from Mujahid: "Those before them" refers to the polytheists at the Battle of Badr.

The "min" here is extra (za'idah), to emphasize the connection of the adverbial expression with its governing element.

"Qarīban" (recently) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, related to the implied "being" (al-kawn al-mudmar) in His saying "ka-mathali" (like), meaning "like a condition that is recent." Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "alladhina" (those), meaning "the people who are near to them," like His saying: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [Hud: 89].

Al-wabal (the evil consequence) originally means the lush pasture that is harmful to livestock when they graze on it; it is said: "kala' wabil" when it is green pasture (sweet), toward which camels hasten, and it then destroys them, makes them ill, or kills them. Thus they, in their advancing to fight the Muslims while ignorant of the outcome of that war, are likened to camels that rushed upon a harmful pasture and perished. The tasting (dhawq) is attributed to it by way of metaphor (makniyya) and its imagining (takhyil), so the mention of "dhaqu" together with "wabal" is an indication of this metaphor.

"Amrihim" (their affair) is their situation and what they plotted and calculated for; that is, they brought themselves into exile (al-jala') and abandoning their homes and what was in them. That is, they tasted the evil of their deeds in this world.

The pronoun in "wa lahum 'adhabun alim" (and for them is a painful punishment) refers to "alladhina min qablihim," meaning: in addition to what they tasted of the punishment of this world through exile and the hardship it entailed upon their souls and bodies, for them is a painful punishment in the Hereafter for disbelief.

[p. 109]

This is another example for another party being likened, and it is not an example joined to the preceding one. Had it been, it would have been conjoined to it with *wa* (and) or *aw* (or), as in His saying: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ (al-Baqarah: 19).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 18:**

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

This is a transition from the favour Allah bestowed upon the Muslims by granting them the conquest of the town of the Banu al-Nadir without fighting, and by giving His Messenger ﷺ what He returned to him from them (fay'), together with a description of what befell them of defeat and of the disappointment of their hopes in the support of the hypocrites. It also contains an indication that the fate of the people of the remaining towns will be like the fate of their predecessors. Likewise is the stance of their helpers with them. It then turns to addressing those who believed with the command to fear Allah, in gratitude to Him for what He has granted and for what He has promised of a true promise. For gratitude is the servant's recompense for his Lord's blessing, since he cannot provide any recompense other than that.

Since what the surah contains of Allah's support for them and the abundance of His blessings upon them belongs to the benefits of this world, He followed it with a reminder to them to prepare for the Hereafter, by His saying ﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, meaning: let each soul consider what it has put forward for the Hereafter.

The clause ﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾ is a conjunction (al-'atf) of one command upon another command. It is placed in between the clause "fear Allah" and the clause ﴿indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾. The mention of "soul" (nafs) is an explicit noun in a place where a pronoun would be expected, for the expected form would be "and look at what you have put forward." He turned away from the pronoun to intend generality, meaning: "let you look," and "let every soul look."

The indefiniteness of "soul" (nafs) conveys generality in the context of a command, meaning: let every soul look. For a command, a supplication and the like are like a conditional, in that an indefinite noun in their context has the same force as it has in a negative context, as in His saying ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6], and as in the words of al-Hariri:

*O people of this abode, may you be spared harm*

meaning "every harm." It was not defined with the definite article to convey generality, lest it be assumed to refer to a known soul.

"Tomorrow" (ghad) is used for the future time by way of metaphor (majaz), to bring the distant future close, because nearness of time is associated with the concept of "tomorrow." For "tomorrow" is the day that follows the day in which the speaker is, so it is the nearest of the future times, as Qurad ibn Ajda' said:

*If the beginning of this day has passed away,*
*then tomorrow is near to the one who looks for it.*

This metaphor is common in Arabic usage with the word "ghad" and its counterparts. Zuhayr said:

*I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it,*
*but as for the knowledge of what is in tomorrow, I am blind to it.*

He means by "today" the present time, by "yesterday" the past time, and by "tomorrow" the future time.

The indefiniteness of "ghad" is for magnification and awe, meaning: for a tomorrow whose reality is not known.

The "lam" in His saying "for tomorrow" (li-ghad) is the lam of cause (lam al-'illa), meaning: what it has put forward for the sake of the Day of Resurrection, that is, for the sake of benefiting from it.

"Putting forward" (taqdim) is used metaphorically for the deed that is done to achieve its benefit at a future time. It likens the intention to benefit from it in the future to the sending ahead of one who will settle in a lodging before travellers arrive at it, whether an army or a caravan, so that he may prepare for them what will set their affairs in order. From this comes the "vanguard" of an army, and the sending ahead of the scout before the caravan. Allah says: ﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110]. Its opposite is said to be "to delay" (akhkhara), when one leaves off doing something. Allah says: ﴿A soul will know what it has put forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5].

The repetition of "And fear Allah" is so that ﴿indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ may be built upon it, so that a connection is achieved between the cause and the caused, since a separation came between them by ﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾. It was repeated by way of conjunction in order to add emphasis, for verbal emphasis is sometimes brought in conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to you, and woe; then woe to you, and woe﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34], and His saying ﴿No! You will soon know. Then no! You will soon know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3–4], and the words of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*He found her saying falsehood and lying.*

This is because conjunction gives the impression that the emphasis is treated as if it were a new statement, adding importance to what is emphasized.

Thus the clause ﴿indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ is a justification for the exhortation to fear Allah, and the position of "indeed" (inna) in it is the position of a justification.

It is also possible that the first "fear Allah" is intended in the sense of fear of Allah, which is what moves one to act, and for this reason it is followed by ﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾. The second "fear Allah" is then intended to mean persistence in the first taqwa, meaning: "persist in fearing Allah," in the manner of His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. For this reason it is followed by ﴿indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, meaning: according to the measure of your striving in taqwa. It is also followed by ﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He caused them to forget themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 19], meaning: they neglected taqwa after they had taken it up, as will come, that they are the hypocrites, for they took up Islam and then wasted it. Allah says: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67].

In His saying ﴿indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ there is the explicit mention of the Name of Majesty (Allah) in a place where a pronoun would be expected, so that the sentence is self-sufficient in its indication in the fullest way, and it works like proverbs. It also serves to cultivate reverence in the hearts of those addressed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 19:

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He caused them to forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

After commanding the believers to be mindful of Allah (taqwa) and to prepare provision for the Hereafter, He followed it with this prohibition as a warning against turning away from the religion and neglecting taqwa, which leads to transgression (fusuq). The prohibition was expressed by forbidding them from the condition of a people in whom this connection was realized, so that the prohibition against neglecting taqwa would be depicted in a tangible form: the form of a people in whom that connection was realized, namely those who turned away from taqwa.

This turning away has degrees, which may reach disbelief (kufr), in which the Jews were involved, and hypocrisy (nifaq), in which a group of those who showed Islam in the early years of the Hijra were involved. The apparent reading of the relative clause is that it refers to a known group, so it is possible that by ﴿those who forgot Allah﴾ the hypocrites are meant, because they were polytheists and had not been guided to monotheism by the guidance of Islam. He expressed hypocrisy by forgetting Allah, because it is ignorance of the attributes of Allah, of monotheism and perfection. He described them as "the defiantly disobedient" in the words of the Most High: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He caused them to forget themselves. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawba: 67] in Surat Bara'a, so this verse looks back to that.

It is also possible that the intended people are the Jews, because they neglected their religion, did not accept the message of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning is: they forgot the religion of Allah and His covenant which He made with them. The Most High said: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant, and fear Me. And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ [al-Baqara: 40].

Their forgetting has been applied to abandonment and deliberate turning away, that is: they forgot the proofs of the oneness of Allah, the proofs of His attributes, the proofs of the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ), and understanding of His Book. So the speech contains an elision of one or two possessives (mudaf).

The meaning of "He caused them to forget themselves" is that Allah did not create in their faculties the awareness to understand the Islamic guidance so that they would act on what saves them from the punishment of the Hereafter and what is good for them in this world. He abandoned them due to the vacillation of their opinions, so the Jews came under the power of the Muslims who expelled them from their homes, and the hypocrites became objects of blame: among the Jews for treachery and breaking covenants, and among the Muslims for contempt and cursing.

The particle fa' of causation indicates that Allah's causing them to forget themselves is a consequence of their forgetting the religion of Allah. That is, when they turned away from guidance by their own acquisition and will, Allah punished them by creating in them forgetfulness of themselves.

The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty in the words of the Most High ﴿like those who forgot Allah﴾, rather than saying "forgot Him", is to express the enormity of this forgetting, so it attached the forgetting to the Name of Allah, who created them and guided them.

The restriction derived from the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) in the words ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ is an ascriptive restriction (qasr idda'i), for the sake of emphasis in describing them with intense fisq, to the extent that the fisq of others seems not to be fisq in comparison with theirs.

The demonstrative noun ("those") is for publicly identifying them by this description.

Fisq (fusuq) is going out of the place appropriate for a thing. It is generally a term of blame, because it is departure from the place fitting for a thing. From it comes the saying: "fasaqat al-rutaba" when the date came out of its skin. So the fasiqun are those who commit the vilest evil deeds and worst bad actions, the greatest of which is associating partners with Allah.

The sentence ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), explaining the ambiguity conveyed by His words "so He caused them to forget themselves," as if the listener asked: "What followed Allah causing them to forget themselves?" It is answered that by this they reached the extreme of fisq in evil deeds, to the point that it became necessary to say: there is no fisq after their fisq.
