**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Surah 59, verse 20:**

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise. The companions of Paradise are the ones who triumph.﴾

This is a *tadhyīl* (a concluding appendage, a sentence that restates and confirms a preceding statement) to the sentence ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 18], and so on. It is because it gathers the essence of the outcome of both states: the state of God-consciousness and preparation for the Hereafter, and the state of forgetting that and neglecting it. For each of the two groups is the outcome of its own deeds. It includes both groups and those like them.

The sentence is also a *faldhalah* (a summary or conclusion) of what precedes it concerning the state of the God-conscious and of those who forgot Allah and whom Allah caused to forget themselves. This is because mentioning this kind of statement after describing the states of the one spoken about generally serves as an indirect rebuke of that person. Like your saying, when you see someone harming people, "The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." So the meaning of the verse is a *kināya* (an allusion, a figure of speech in which the intended meaning is implied) to the fact that the believers are the companions of Paradise, and that those who forgot Allah are the people of the Fire. Thus the verse contains a promise to the God-conscious and a warning to the wicked.

Page 115

The purpose of negating equality in such a context is the *kināya* to the great distance between the two things.

Determining which of the two things is preferred is left to the listener's understanding from the context of the situation, as in the saying of al-Samaw'al:

*So the knower and the ignorant are not equal.*

And the saying of Abū Ḥizām Ghālib ibn al-Ḥārith al-ʿUklī:

*And I know that submission and abandonment*
*are neither alike nor equal.*

From this is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They are not equal﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 113], after His saying ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110] and so on. It has been said that it refers to His saying ﴿Among the People of the Book is a standing community﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 113]. The negation is sometimes followed by something indicating the direction of preference, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; they are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 10]. And His saying here, ﴿The companions of Paradise are the ones who triumph.﴾ And it has preceded in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Not equal are the believers who sit [at home]﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 95], the verse in Surah al-Nisāʾ.

As for those among the scholars of *uṣūl* (the principles of Islamic jurisprudence) who went to generalize expressions such as *lā yastawūn* (they are not equal) from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a defiant transgressor? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajdah: 18], and used it as evidence that the wicked person may not exercise guardianship in marriage (*wilāyat al-nikāḥ*), which is the argument of the Shāfiʿiyyah, then that is not an acceptable conclusion. The Ḥanafiyyah have rejected it, and Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī agreed with them in *Ghayr Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ*.

The restriction (*qaṣr*) derived from the separating pronoun (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*, the pronoun هُمْ placed between the subject and predicate) in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿The companions of Paradise are the ones who triumph﴾, is a *qaṣr iddiʿāʾī* (a restriction by claim, a figurative restriction), because their triumph is everlasting, so the triumph of others is considered, by comparison with some worldly matters, as nothing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 21:

﴿If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, split apart out of fear of God. And these are the parables We set forth for mankind, that perhaps they may reflect.﴾

When He warned the believers against falling into the abyss of forgetting God, into which the defiant ones (al-fasiqun) had fallen, and threatened those who forgot God with the Fire, and explained their condition by saying that Satan had made disbelief appealing to them... The Qur'an was guiding to the paths of good and warning against the paths of evil, and the defiant ones had fallen into ruin only because of their neglect of reflecting upon it, and that was due to their forgetting God, the Exalted. The discourse moved on to praising the Qur'an and its clear guidance, which only their desires and their obstinacy turn people away from, and their aversion to it was the root of the continuation of their misguidance and their polytheism. He set forth this parable to express wonder at their stubbornness in misguidance.

In this transition there is also an indication that the surah is ending, because it is a shift after a long discourse on the subject of the conquest of the Jewish settlements and what the hypocrites suffer as a consequence of loss in this world and the Hereafter.

"This Qur'an" points to the portion of it that was revealed, which is what they knew, recited, and heard recited.

The purpose of using the demonstrative for the near is to imply to them that the Qur'an is not far from them, that it is within their reach, and that reflecting upon it is no burden for them; but they chose to turn away from it.

This is a parable which God set forth, as indicated by His saying "And these are the parables" etc. It was set forth as an example of the hardness of those who forgot God and of their being unaffected by the striking admonitions of the Qur'an.

By "the mountain" is meant its literal sense, because the discourse is a supposition and hypothesis, as is required by the use of "law" (if) in hypothetical conditions.

So the mountain is an example of the hardest of things and of the least affected by what strikes it. The sending down of the Qur'an is a metaphor for addressing it with it. It was expressed as "sending down" by way of consequence, likening the nobility of a thing to the height of a place, and for conveying it to others by the image of a thing being sent down from a height.

The meaning: if the one addressed by the Qur'an were a mountain, and the mountain could understand the address, it would be affected by the Qur'an's address with an effect arising from fear of God, a fear that the meanings of the Qur'an would impress upon it.

The meaning is also: if the mountain were in the position of these who forgot God, turned away from understanding the Qur'an, and were not admonished by its exhortations, the mountain would have been admonished, its rock and soil would have split apart from the intensity of its being affected by the fear of God.

"Splitting apart" is given as a parable for the intensity of emotion and being affected, because the ultimate effect upon solid bodies is that they break and split, since that does not happen to them easily.

The "khushu'" (humbling) is lowering and bowing, that is, you would see its upper part descending to the earth.
The "tasaddu'" (splitting) is cracking, that is, it would quake and crack out of its fear of God, the Exalted.

The address in "you would have seen it" is to an unspecified person, so it includes everyone who hears this discourse. The seeing is visual, and it is negated because it follows the particle "law" (if) of impossibility.

The meaning: if it were so, you would have seen the mountain in a state of humbling and splitting.

The sentence "And these are the parables We set forth for mankind" is a concluding remark (tadhyil), because what preceded it was presented in the manner of a parable, so it was concluded by saying that the parables God sets forth in His speech are like this parable, and He intends by them that they reflect. If they do not reflect upon them, their obstinacy and stubbornness have been recorded against them. So the reference in "these" is to the totality of the many parables that passed before their ears, and the implied sense is: We have set forth this parable, and these parables We set forth for mankind.

"Darb al-mathal" (setting forth a parable) means presenting it. The verb "darb" was used in the sense of placing, as one says "he built (daraba) a house," and the explanation of this has already passed at His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed God is not ashamed to set forth any parable" [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 59, verse 22:

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾

When the name of Allah, His pronouns, and His attributes were repeated in this surah forty times, twenty-four of them by the name of majesty (ism al-jalala, "Allah") and sixteen by an apparent pronoun referring to Him or by His exalted attributes, and when what the surah contains constitutes evidence of the great power of Allah, the wonder of His disposal of affairs, and His wisdom, and when what the surah contains is a lesson about the great power of Allah, in that He strengthened the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims and granted them victory over the Banu al-Nadir, a victory that broke with custom, and it mentioned what befell the hypocrites, their helpers, and that this was because they opposed Allah and His Messenger, and this was countered by praise of the believers in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ who supported the religion; then came the command to obey Allah and prepare for the Day of Recompense, and the warning against those who turned away from the Book of Allah and against the evil of their end; and this was concluded with a reminder of the Qur'an, which indicates what is good and makes known the greatness of Allah, which necessitates intense fear of Him; he followed this by mentioning a group of the great attributes of Allah, which have numerous effects in His dealings, appropriate to the purpose of the surah, as an increase in making the believers know His greatness, which necessitates further fear of Him, and by the beautiful attributes which necessitate love of Him, and as an increase in frightening the stubborn opponents who turn away, from the attributes of His might and sovereignty; and for this reason He mentioned in these concluding verses of the surah, from His attributes, the Exalted, what is of varying relation and effect for the two groups, each receiving what is fitting for it from them.

Throughout all of this there is evidence of the falsity of their associating idols with Him. We will mention the references of these names to what the surah includes later on.

The pronoun of absence (ḍamīr al-ghayba) occurring at the beginning of the sentence refers to the name of majesty in His saying (O you who believe, fear Allah). "Huwa" (He) is the subject (mubtada'), the name of majesty is the predicate (khabar) about it, and "alladhi" (who/the one who) is an attribute (ṣifa) of the name of majesty.

The apparent requirement would have been to limit the reference to the pronoun without mentioning the name of majesty, because the intended purpose is to inform about the pronoun by (who there is no deity other than Him) and what follows of exalted attributes. So the combination of the pronoun with what is equivalent to it (the name of majesty) carries the consideration that the name of majesty gathers all the attributes of perfection, because its root is al-Ilah (the Deity), and the meaning of al-Ilah requires the gathering of all attributes of perfection.

It is also permissible that the pronoun be a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun referring to the matter or situation under discussion), and the speech is then a new sentence (isti'naf) intended to teach the Muslims these attributes so that they may reflect upon them, and to refute the polytheists who associate with the One possessing these attributes other things of which none has any share of such attributes. For this reason a group of them was concluded with the sentence (Glory be to Allah above what they associate) [al-Hashr: 23], so that it would be a seal for this noble surah, which contained a great favour, namely the favour of the victory that had occurred and the easy conquest in the future. Undoubtedly it is fitting that they should know the sublime attributes of Him, whose relations have effects in the present circumstances and in the conquests that will yet come, and that the polytheists and the disbelieving Jews should know that their defeats followed one after another only because of their disbelief. Since the matter of these attributes is great, it was appropriate that the sentence begin with the pronoun of the matter, so that the name of majesty is the subject and "alladhi la ilaha illa huwa" (who there is no deity other than Him) is the predicate. The sentence is then a predicate for the pronoun of the matter.

The discussion of these exalted attributes began with the attribute of oneness (al-wahdaniyya), which is the meaning of (who there is no deity other than Him), and it is the foundation for what follows of attributes. For this reason its mention occurs frequently in the Qur'an immediately after the name of majesty, as in the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi) and the opening of Al 'Imran.

It was followed by the attribute of Knower of the unseen, because it is what the attribute of divinity (al-ilahiyya) requires, since the knowledge of Allah is the necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-wajib), and it requires all the attributes, since the reality of necessary knowledge is not established except by the negative attributes, and since it requires the attributes of meaning (al-ma'nawiyya). Among the objects of His knowledge are the matters of the unseen, because it is by this that the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is distinguished from the knowledge of others. He mentioned along with it the knowledge of the witnessed as a safeguard against the supposition that He knows only the lofty universal realities, as one group of the ancient philosophers held. Also, the definiteness in "the unseen and the witnessed" is for totality (al-istighraq), meaning every unseen and every witnessed, and that is something no other shares with Him. It is the knowledge of the unseen and the witnessed, that is, of what is absent from people's perception and what is present to them. So the intended sense here is that of the active participle: the Knower of what appears and what is hidden from them, of every hidden thing to which knowledge relates, as it is.

The definiteness in "the unseen and the witnessed" is for true totality (al-istighraq al-haqiqi).

In the mention of the unseen there is an allusion to the misguidance of those who confined themselves to what is observed and disbelieved in the unseen matters of resurrection, recompense, and the sending of the messengers. As for the mention of the knowledge of the witnessed, it is a completion, since the polytheists suppose that Allah does not perceive what they conceal. He the Exalted said: (You did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins testify against you) [Fussilat: 22], up to His saying (among the losers).

The pronoun in (He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful) is a separating pronoun (ḍamir al-fasl), which indicates the restriction of mercy to Him the Exalted, since the mercy of others is not counted because of its deficiency. He the Exalted said: (My mercy encompasses all things) [al-A'raf: 156]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah placed mercy in one hundred parts, and He kept ninety-nine parts with Himself and sent down one part to the earth. From that one part the creation shows mercy to one another, to the extent that the horse lifts its hoof from its foal out of fear that it might harm it." The discussion of al-Rahman and al-Rahim has already preceded in the surah al-Fatiha.

The reason for placing the attribute of the comprehensiveness of knowledge before the attribute of mercy is that the comprehensiveness of knowledge requires that nothing of the circumstances of His creation and their need for Him be hidden from His knowledge. So He shows mercy to those who are in need of His mercy, and He grants respite to the stubborn opponents until the punishment of the Hereafter. Thus He is merciful toward them in this world. The name of majesty has frequently been followed by the two attributes al-Rahman and al-Rahim in the Qur'an, as in al-Fatiha.

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supreme.﴾

The discussion of the pronoun هو (huwa) is like the discussion of its counterpart in the first clause. This is a repetition for resumption (al-tikrar li-l-istiʾnaf), because the context is one of exaltation, and that is one of the contexts of repetition. It also shows concern with the attribute of oneness (al-wahdaniyya).

Al-Malik (the King) is the one who rules over people. There is no king in the absolute sense except Allah, Exalted is He. As for describing others as king, it is relative to a specific group of people. The two attributes of mercy are followed by the attribute of sovereignty (al-mulk) to indicate that His mercy is a bounty and that He has absolute freedom of disposal, as occurs in Surat al-Fatiha.

Al-Quddus (the Most Holy) is pronounced with a ḍamma on the qāf (القُدُّوسُ) in the most eloquent form, though the qāf may also be pronounced with a fatḥa. Ibn Jinnī said: the pattern faʿʿūl in adjectives is rare; it occurs mainly in nouns, such as tannūr (oven), saffūd (a type of fishing hook/spit), and ʿabbūd. Sībawayh mentioned السَّبُّوحُ (al-Subbūḥ) with a fatḥa. Thaʿlab said that the pattern fuʿʿūl with a ḍamma on its first letter does not occur except in al-Quddūs and al-Subbūḥ. Others added al-Dhurrūḥ, which is a red fly with reddish patches mixed with black, resembling the wasp; in the terminology of physicians it is called dhubāb al-Hind (the Indian fly). All other such words have a fatḥa, like saffūd, kallub, tannūr, samūr, and shabbūṭ (a kind of fish). It seems he means that al-Subbūḥ and al-Quddūs have become proper names.

Following al-Malik with al-Quddus is a safeguard (iḥtirās), indicating that He is free of the known defects of kings, such as arrogance, indulgence in desires, and similar defects of the soul.

Al-Salām is a verbal noun meaning peace (al-musālama). Allah Exalted is described by it in the manner of describing by a verbal noun for emphasis, meaning "the One possessing peace," that is, safety (al-salāma). This is that He Exalted kept creation safe from injustice and oppression. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah is al-Salām, and peace comes from Him."
[Page 121]
Thus the placement of al-Salām after al-Malik is clear. After He followed with al-Quddus to show the purity of His essence, He followed with al-Salām to show justice in His dealings with creation. This too is a safeguard. Al-Muʾmin is the active participle of āmana, whose hamza is for causation (al-taʿdiya), meaning He made another secure.

So Allah is the One who placed security in most states of existing things, for He created the order of creation far from dangers and calamities. Calamities befall creatures only through accidental causes that arise from concurrence, opposition, or conflict of interests, so the stronger is preferred and the weaker is repelled. Sometimes they come as a result of people's actions.

Mentioning al-Muʾmin after the attributes before it completes the safeguard against the assumption that describing Him as al-Malik means He is like the kings known for their defects. So first the purity of His essence is established by al-Quddus, then the purity of His hidden dealings from deceit and plotting by al-Muʾmin, and then the purity of His manifest dealings from tyranny and injustice by al-Salām.

Al-Muhaymin: the watcher (al-raqīb) in the dialect of Quraysh, and the guardian (al-ḥāfiẓ) in the dialect of the rest of the Arabs.

Its derivation has been disputed. It has been said that it is derived from āmana, with the causative hamza entering it, so it became āmana, and the pattern of the attribute is muʾaymin, whose hamza was changed to hāʾ. The reason for the change is probably the intention to transfer it from the adjectival to the nominal category, regardless of the meaning of security, so that it became like a fixed noun. Its meaning became "watched over." Do you not see that no meaning remains in it except that which is in al-Muʾmin, once it became a name for the watcher and the witness? This is a rare change, like the change of the hamza in أراق (arāqa, to pour) to hāʾ, so they said هَراقَ (harāqa). Al-Jawharī placed it in the section of the hamza in the chapter of the nūn, and its pattern is mufaʿlil, an active participle of āmana like mudaḥrij. Its inflection would be mu'ʾamin with two hamzas after the first, added mīm; the first hamza was changed to hāʾ, as the hamza of أراق was changed, so they said هَراقَ.

It has also been said that its root is هَيْمَنَ (haymana), meaning "watched over," as in Lisān al-ʿArab. Accordingly, the hāʾ is original and the pattern is mufayʿil. Ṣāḥib al-Qāmūs mentioned it in the section of the hāʾ in the chapter of the nūn, and did not mention it in the section of the hamza. Al-Jawharī mentioned it in the section of the hamza and in the section of the hāʾ in the chapter of the nūn, explicitly stating that its hāʾ originally was a hamza. Al-Rāghib and the author of al-Asās avoided mentioning it.
[Page 122]
That indicates that they both regard its hāʾ as changed from a hamza, and that it falls within the meanings of security. In al-Maqṣad al-Asnā fī Sharḥ Asmāʾ Allāh al-Ḥusnā by al-Ghazālī, al-Muhaymin regarding Allah means: the One who oversees His creation in their deeds and sustenance. His oversight is through His knowledge, His dominance, and His preservation. Watching over (al-ishrāf, which is knowledge) goes back to knowledge, dominance goes back to perfect power, and preservation goes back to action. The name al-Muhaymin combines these meanings, and no one can combine that perfection and absoluteness except Allah Exalted; for this reason it has been said that it is one of the names of Allah in the earlier scriptures. End of quotation. In this definition with this detail there is room for review, and perhaps Ḥujjat al-Islām meant it as a consideration of the attribute rather than an explanation of its meaning.

The placement of al-Muhaymin after al-Muʾmin serves to remove the assumption that His granting security is from weakness or from fear of others. Know that His granting security is by His wisdom, even though He is a watcher who is aware of the conditions of His creation. Thus His granting them security is mercy toward them.

Al-ʿAzīz (the Almighty) is the One who cannot be overcome and whom no one can humble, and for this reason He has been interpreted as al-Ghālib (the Victorious).

Al-Jabbār (the Compeller) is the One who overpowers and forces others to be affected by His action. So Allah is the compeller of every creature in its actions, because of what He has formed it upon. No creature can transgress what He has set for it in its creation. Man cannot fly, and quadrupeds cannot walk on two legs only. Likewise He is the Compeller of existing things in accepting what He wills for them and what His power has decreed upon them.

When man is described as jabbār, it is a term of blame, because it implies that he compels others to his own desires. For this reason Allah Exalted said: ﴿If you wish only to be a tyrant in the land and not to be among the reformers﴾ [al-Qasas: 19]. So jabbār is one of the forms of intensity, because it is derived from ajbara, and forms of intensity are derived from the augmented form rarely, like al-Ḥakīm in the sense of al-Muḥkim. Al-Farrāʾ said: "I have not heard faʿʿāl from afʿala except jabbār and darrāk." The analogy would have been to say al-mujbir and al-mudrik. It has been said that jabbār means "the one who mends," from jabara al-kasr (he set the break), when he repaired it. Its derivation then has no oddity.

Al-Mutakabbir (the Supreme) is the one of greatest majesty (al-kibriyāʾ), that is, grandeur and sublimity. The original function of the form tafaʿʿul is to indicate affectation (al-takallluf), but here it is used for its necessary consequence, which is strength, because an act issuing from refinement and effort is more perfect.
[Page 123]
It is said: فُلانُ يَتَظَلَّمُ عَلى النّاسِ (so-and-so oppresses the people), meaning he greatly increases their oppression.

The reason these three attributes are mentioned after the attribute al-Muhaymin is that all the attributes mentioned above indicate only that the servants may be at peace in the care of their Lord and the reform of their affairs. The attribute al-Muhaymin indicates a common matter, so it was followed by the attribute al-ʿAzīz, so that people would know that Allah is Victorious, and nothing can frustrate Him. It was followed by the attribute al-Jabbār, which indicates that He subjects creatures to His will, then the attribute al-Mutakabbir, which indicates that He is the Possessor of greatness, before whose majesty everything is small. Thus these attributes are on the side of warning, just as the attributes before them were on the side of encouragement.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ These attributes are concluded with the declaration of Allah's transcendence above having partners, by the association the polytheists made with Him. The pronoun in يُشْرِكُونَ (they associate) refers to something known from the context, namely the polytheists, whom the Qur'an has continued to rebuke with admonitions.

[Page 124]

﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾. The discussion of the pronoun "He" (*huwa*) with which the verse opens, and of the repetition of the clause, is the same as the discussion of the one preceding it. If the third-person pronoun is a pronoun of *sha'n* (the pronoun of matter or situation), then the clause following it is its predicate.

The clause "Allah, the Creator" (*Allahu al-Khaliq*) conveys a restriction (*qasr*, exclusivity) by way of definiteness of both parts of the sentence: He is the Creator, not their partners. This is a refutation of the divinity of that which does not create. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those you invoke besides Allah do not create anything, and they are themselves created﴾ [An-Nahl: 20], and He said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not be reminded?﴾ [An-Nahl: 17]. If the pronoun refers back to the previously mentioned name Allah, then the name Allah after it is the predicate, and "the Creator" (*al-Khaliq*) is an attribute.

[Page 125]

*Al-Khaliq* is an active participle from *al-khalq* (creation). The basic meaning of *al-khalq* in the language is the bringing into existence of a thing in a specific form. This was already discussed under His, exalted is He, words relating the words of Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I create for you from clay like the form of a bird﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 49], the verse in Surat Ali 'Imran. The term *khalq* is also used in a more specific sense than the bringing into existence of forms, namely the bringing into existence of that which did not exist before, as in His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [Qaf: 38]. This is the predominant meaning when the name of Allah, exalted is He, "the Creator," is used.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "the one who determines what He brings into existence." He quoted from him, in explaining what he meant by this, that he said: "Since Allah's originations are determined by measures of wisdom, He expressed His origination by *khalq*." This indicates that *al-Khaliq* as an attribute of Allah means the one who originates things from non-existence, and by this *khalq* is more general than *taswir* (fashioning). The mention of *al-Bari'* and *al-Musawwir* after *al-Khaliq* is then an alert to particular states within creation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ [Al-A'raf: 11], according to one of the two interpretations.

Al-Raghib said: "*Al-khalq* is precise determination (*al-taqdir al-mustaqim*), and it is used for the placing of a thing [into existence] without a prior material or a model."

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said in *'Aridat al-Ahwadhi* on the *Sunan* of al-Tirmidhi: "*Al-Khaliq* is the one who brings things out from non-existence into existence, with their attributes determined for them." He then mixed the two meanings. Then he said: "*Al-Khaliq* is general, *al-Bari'* is more specific than it, and *al-Musawwir* is more specific than the more specific." This is close to the words of the author of *al-Kashshaf*.

Al-Ghazali said in *al-Maqsad al-Asna*: "*Al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir* may be thought to be synonymous names, but this should not be the case. Rather, everything that comes out from non-existence into existence requires first a determination, second bringing into existence in accordance with that determination, and third fashioning after its bringing into existence. Allah is *Khaliq* insofar as He is the determiner, *Bari'* insofar as He is the one who innovates and brings into existence, and *Musawwir* insofar as He arranges the forms of the innovated things in the best arrangement." So he made the meanings mutually implicating and made the difference between them one of perspective. I do not think this applies to the actual usages of these names.

*Al-Bari'* is an active participle from *bara'a* (with a hamza). Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "The one who distinguishes what He brings into existence from one another by their different shapes." This differs from the specific meaning of *al-Khaliq*.

[Page 126]

In a hadith: "from the evil of what He created, originated (*dhara'a*) and produced (*bara'a*)." And from the words of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "No, by the One who split the grain and produced (*bara'a*) the soul." So the term *al-bariyyah* is not restricted to human beings in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the worst of creation (*al-bariyyah*)﴾ and ﴿Those are the best of creation (*al-bariyyah*)﴾. Al-Raghib said: "*Al-bariyyah*: creation."

Ibn al-'Arabi said in *al-'Aridah*: "*Al-Bari'* is the one who creates human beings from *al-bara* (clay, dust) (with the vowel pronounced short), and it is specific to the creation of the human species. On this view, the term *al-bariyyah* is specific to mankind in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the worst of creation﴾ and ﴿Those are the best of creation﴾."

Ibn 'Atiyyah explained it with the meaning of *al-Khaliq*, and so did the author of *al-Qamus*. Al-Ghazali explained it as "the existent, the innovator." You have learned that this does not apply, so the best explanation of it is what is in *al-Kashshaf*.

*Al-Musawwir* is the one who forms the forms of all created things that have visible forms.

These attributes were mentioned in sequence because from their totality one obtains a conception of the divine originating for human beings: one begins with *khalq*, which is the primary bringing into existence; then with *bara'*, which is the forming of the human body; then with *taswir*, which is the giving of a good form, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The One who created you and proportioned you and balanced you, in whatever form He willed﴾ [Al-Infitar: 7–8], and ﴿He who fashions you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6].

The purpose of their mention right after the preceding attributes, that is, of these three attributes, is to indicate His disposition over human beings through bringing them into existence in His wondrous manner, so as to stir in them the motive to give thanks for that. For this reason, they are followed by the clause ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾.

Know that the way of relating these excellent attributes to what suits them from the contents of the surah divides into three categories, but they are mentioned in the verse according to the appropriateness of the placement of some of them after others, through contrast (*tanzir*), precaution (*ihtiras*), or completion (*tatmim*), as you have just learned.

The first category relates to what suits the conditions of the polytheists and their allies, the Jews, who banded together against the Prophet ﷺ and against the Muslims with war, scheming, and harm, and to their supporters among the hypocrites who deceived the Muslims.

[Page 127]

To this category belongs the attribute "There is no god but He." This attribute is the basis for readiness to reflect upon and contemplate the rest of the attributes, for polytheism is the root of misguidance. The polytheists are those who incited the Jews, and the hypocrites were between the Jews and the polytheists, concealing themselves by displaying Islam. Thus shirk is what barred people from reaching the paths of guidance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they added nothing to them except ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

Also the attribute "Knower of the unseen" (*'alim al-ghayb*), for among the roots of shirk is denying the unseen, whose consequences include denying resurrection and recompense, persisting in error and committing misdeeds, and denying revelation and prophethood. This looks back to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾ [Al-Hashr: 4], and what follows.

Likewise the mention of the attributes "the King" (*al-Malik*), "the Mighty" (*al-'Aziz*), "the Compeller" (*al-Jabbar*), and "the Majestic" (*al-Mutakabbir*), because they correspond to what He sent down upon the Banu al-Nadir of terror, humiliation, and seizing.

The second category relates to what the believers gathered as fruit of victory in the story of the Banu al-Nadir. These are the attributes: "the Giver of Peace" (*al-Salam*), "the Bestower of Security" (*al-Mu'min*), corresponding to His saying: ﴿So you did not press forward against it with horses or camels﴾ [Al-Hashr: 6], meaning the Muslims did not undergo hardship, harm, or fighting to obtain the spoils.

Likewise the two attributes "the Most Merciful" (*al-Rahman*) and "the Most Compassionate" (*al-Rahim*), because of their suitability for giving a share of the *fay'* (spoils acquired without battle) to the weak.

The third category relates to what both parties mentioned in this surah share, so each party takes its portion of them. These are the attributes: "the Holy" (*al-Quddus*), "the Guardian" (*al-Muhaymin*), "the Creator" (*al-Khaliq*), "the Evolver" (*al-Bari'*), "the Fashioner" (*al-Musawwir*).

﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾. This is a conclusion (*tadhyil*) to what has been enumerated of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He. That is, to Him belong all the most beautiful names, of which the attributes mentioned just before are some.

By "names" is meant attributes. He expressed them as names because He is described by them on the tongues of His creatures, and because they reach the ultimate reality of their meanings in relation to His description, exalted is He, so they become like proper names for His essence, exalted is He.

[Page 128]

The intended meaning is that the meanings indicated by the most beautiful names belong to Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 31], after His saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 31]. That is, He presented the named things to the angels.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180] has already been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The clause "glorifies Him" etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in "To Him belong the most beautiful names." That is to say, His possession of the most beautiful attributes compels those rational beings in the heavens and the earth to exalt Him by glorifying and declaring Him free of deficiencies. Thus each category, moved by its knowledge of some of Allah's names, glorifies and declares Him free of imperfection, whether intentionally or unintentionally. So the naturalist or the materialist, when he admires the order of existence and is impressed by its coherence, is in reality glorifying the free-choosing agent, even if he calls it time or nature. This holds when "glorification" is taken in its literal sense, which is declaring Him free of imperfection by speech. But if it is taken to include both the literal and the metaphorical senses, namely indicating exaltation even by the tongue of the state, then the meaning is that the attributes of creating, sustaining, and subduing that belong to Him are indicated by the evidences of created things and the order of their existence.

The clause "and He is the Mighty, the Wise" is coordinated with the circumstantial clause, and these two attributes were chosen because of their strong suitability to the order of creation.

In this verse there is *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (a rhetorical device in which the end of a passage echoes its beginning), because the beginning of the surah corresponds to its end.

Al-Tirmidhi related with a good chain (*sanad hasan*) from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever says three times when he enters the morning: 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan,' and then recites the last three verses of Surat al-Hashr, ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no god, Knower of the unseen﴾ [Al-Hashr: 22] to the end of the surah, Allah appoints seventy thousand angels to send blessings upon him until evening, and if he dies that day he dies as a martyr. And whoever says them when he enters the evening has the same status." This is a virtue of these verses in the hereafter.

[Page 129]

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi related in his *Tarikh* with his chain, from Idris ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Haddad, who said: "I read to Khalaf, the transmitter of Hamzah's reading, and when I reached this verse ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ [Al-Hashr: 21] to the end of the surah, he said: 'Place your hand on your head, for I read to al-A'mash.' When I reached this verse, he said: 'Place your hand on your head, for I read to Yahya ibn Wathhab.' When I reached this verse, he said: 'Place your hand on your head, for I read to 'Alqamah and al-Aswad.' When I reached this verse, he said: 'Place your hand on your head, for we read to 'Abd Allah.' In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Surat al-Mumtahanah. This surah is known in the books of *tafsir* (Qur'anic exegesis) and the books of *Sunnah* (prophetic tradition) and in the mushafs as "Surat al-Mumtahanah." Al-Qurtubi said: "The commonly used pronunciation of the word '*al-Mumtahanah*' is with a kasrah on the *ha'*, and this is what al-Suhayli affirmed decisively."

The reason for the name is that the surah contains the verse on testing the faith of the women who came from Makkah as emigrants to Madinah, namely the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10] up to His saying ﴿the bonds of disbelieving women﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10]. People therefore described that verse as "the Mumtahanah" because it prescribed the testing, and the surah was attributed to that verse.

Al-Suhayli said: "The testing is ascribed to the surah metaphorically, as it was said of Surat Bara'ah that it is 'the Exposer' (*al-Fadihah*)." That is, this description is a metaphorical attribution in the rhetorical sense (*majaz 'aqli*).

It was also transmitted with a fatha on the *ha'*, as a passive participle. Ibn Hajar said: "This is the well-known reading, meaning 'the woman who was tested,' the definite article being the definite of previous reference, referring to the first woman who was tested in her faith, Umm Kulthum daughter of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, wife of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf." Just as the surah of "Qad sami'a Allah" was named "Surat al-Mujadilah" with a kasrah on the *dal*.

You may also make the definite article a definite of genus, that is, "the women who are tested."

This surah is Madani by consensus.

The scholars of enumeration (ahl al-'adad) agreed that its verses number thirteen, and its verses are long.

They agreed that the first verse was revealed concerning the letter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to the polytheists of Makkah.

Al-Bukhari narrated through the route of Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, reaching back to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), the story of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's letter to the people of Makkah. Then he said: 'Amr ibn Dinar said: "It was revealed concerning him: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]." Sufyan said: "This is in the narration of the people; I do not know whether it is in the hadith or in the statement of 'Amr. I memorized it from 'Amr and did not omit a single letter from it." End quote.

In Sahih Muslim, the narrators Abu Bakr and Zuhayr, among the five from whom Muslim narrated, do not mention the verse when narrating from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah. Ishaq, that is Ibn Ibrahim, who is one of those from whom Muslim narrated this hadith, included it in his narration as a recitation of Sufyan. End quote. Muslim did not address the narration of 'Amr al-Naqid and Ibn Abi 'Umar from Sufyan, so perhaps they did not mention anything about it.

They differed concerning the time of his writing to them. Was it when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preparing for al-Hudaybiyah? This is the view of Qatadah, and Ibn 'Atiyyah adopted it, and it is what the narration of al-Harith from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in al-Tabari implies. He said: When the Prophet ﷺ intended to go to Makkah, he spread among the people that he wanted Khaybar, and he confided to some of his companions, among them Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, that he wanted Makkah. So Hatib wrote to the people of Makkah... to the end of it. The statement "he spread that he wanted Khaybar" indicates that his intention toward Makkah was for the 'umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, not for the conquest of Makkah, because Khaybar was conquered before the conquest of Makkah. This is supported by what al-Tabari narrated: that the woman whom Hatib sent with his letter came to Madinah two years after the Battle of Badr. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This surah was revealed in the sixth year.

A group said: Hatib's letter to the people of Makkah was when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preparing for the conquest of Makkah. This is the apparent practice of the majority of historians (ahl al-siyar) and the practice of al-Bukhari in the Book of Campaigns (kitab al-maghazi) of his Sahih in his arrangement of the expeditions, and most exegetes adopted it.

Most of the narrations do not specify what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended by his preparation for Makkah: was it for the 'umrah or for the conquest? If the first view is the more correct one, which is the one we choose, then the entire surah was revealed within a close period, for the testing of Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah took place right after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. The revelation of the surah would then be in the order of its verses, which is the basic principle regarding surahs.

According to the second view, the surah's descent would be after the verses of testing and what follows them, to the point that some said: the beginning of the surah was revealed in Makkah after the conquest. This is a strange view on which one should not rely.

This surah is counted as the ninety-second in the enumeration of the order of the revelation of the surahs, according to Jabir ibn Zayd: it was revealed after Surat al-'Uqud (al-Ma'idah) and before Surat al-Nisa'.

Among its themes: warning the believers against taking the polytheists as allies, although they disbelieved in the true religion and expelled them from their lands.

Informing them that taking them as allies is misguidance, and that if they gained power over the believers they would harm them by deed and word; and that the ties of kinship between them and the polytheists carry no weight in the face of enmity over religion. He gave the example of Ibrahim's severance from his father and his people.

He followed this with reassuring the believers with the hope that affection would arise between them and those whom Allah had commanded them to oppose, meaning this enmity is not permanent.

He followed with permission to treat kindly those disbelievers who did not fight the Muslims in religion and did not expel them from their homes. These rulings extend to the end of the ninth verse.

And the ruling concerning believing women who come as emigrants, testing the sincerity of their faith, that they be protected from returning to the abode of polytheism, that their polytheist husbands be compensated for the dowries they gave them, and that the same restitution be made with the polytheists.
